[Names of the Surah]

Abd al-Rahman ibn Ibrahim ibn Muhammad ibn Yahya informed us; Abu Bakr Muhammad ibn al-Husayn al-Qattan informed us; and Muhammad ibn Ahmad ibn Abdus informed us; Muhammad ibn al-Mu'ammal ibn al-Hasan ibn Isa informed us; al-Fadl ibn Muhammad ibn al-Musayyab narrated to us; Khalaf ibn Hisham narrated to us; Muhammad ibn Hassan narrated to us from al-Mu'afa ibn Imran, from Abd al-Hamid ibn Ja'far al-Ansari, from Sa'id al-Maqbari, from Abu Hurayra, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Al-hamdu lillahi rabbi al-'alamin (Praise be to Allah, Lord of the worlds) are seven verses, the first of which is (In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful). They are the seven oft-repeated (al-sab' al-mathani), they are the Mother of the Qur'an, and they are the Opening of the Book." [Tafsir Ibn Kathir: 1/10, with variation.]

[Its Revelation]

They differed concerning where it was revealed.

Abu al-Qasim al-Hasan ibn Muhammad ibn Ja'far informed us by reading; Abu al-Hasan Muhammad ibn Mahmud ibn Abd Allah al-Marwazi informed us, saying: Abd Allah ibn Mahmud al-Sa'di narrated to us; Abu Yahya al-Qasri narrated to us; Marwan ibn Mu'awiya narrated to us from al-Wala' ibn al-Musayyab, from al-Fadl ibn Amr, from Ali ibn Abi Talib (may Allah be pleased with him), who said: "The Opening of the Book was revealed at Makkah from a treasure beneath the Throne." [Asbab al-Nuzul of al-Wahidi: 11.]

This is the view of most scholars.

What supports it is:

Al-Hasan ibn Muhammad ibn Ja'far informed us; Muhammad ibn Mahmud narrated to us; Abu Lubaba Muhammad ibn Mahdi narrated to us; my father narrated to us, from Sadaqa ibn Abd al-Rahman, from Rawh ibn al-Qasim al-Abari, from Umar ibn Shurahbil, who said: "The first of the Qur'an to be revealed was (Al-hamdu lillahi rabbi al-'alamin), and that is because the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) confided to Khadija (may Allah be pleased with her) and said: 'I have feared that something has come upon me.' She said: 'And what is that?' He said: 'When I am alone, I hear a call, so I flee.' Abu Bakr took him to Waraqa ibn Nawfal, and Waraqa said to him: 'When it comes to you, sit and listen to it.' Then Jibril came to him and said: 'Say: In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful. Al-hamdu lillahi rabbi al-'alamin.'" [With variation in Asbab al-Nuzul of al-Wahidi: 11.] [6]

And al-Hasan ibn Ja'far narrated to us; Muhammad ibn Mahmud narrated to us; Amr ibn Salih narrated to us from Ibn Abbas; my father narrated to us from al-Kalbi, from Abu Salih, from Ibn Abbas, who said: The Prophet (ﷺ) stood in Makkah and said: In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful. Al-hamdu lillahi rabbi al-'alamin. The Quraysh said: "May Allah split your mouth." [In the original, written above it: "Raqq" (rather than "Daqq").]

Abu al-Qasim al-Hasan ibn Muhammad ibn al-Hasan informed us; Abu Muhammad Abd Allah ibn Muhammad ibn Ya'qub informed us; Abu Zayd narrated to us; Abu Hatim ibn Mahbub al-Shami narrated to us; Abd al-Jabbar al-Ala' informed us, from Ma'n, from Mansur, from Mujahid, who said: "The Opening of the Book was revealed at Madina."

al-Hasan ibn al-Fadl said: "Every scholar has a lapse, and this report from Mujahid is rejected, because he alone transmitted it, and the scholars are against it."

The report from the Prophet (ﷺ) is authentic in the hadith of Ubayy ibn Ka'b that it is among: "the first of the Qur'an to be revealed," and that it is: "the seven oft-repeated" [Sunan al-Darimi: 2/445] [8]. And Surat al-Hijr is Makkan without disagreement. It is well known that Allah did not bestow favour upon him by giving him the seven oft-repeated while he was in Makkah and then revealing them at Madina; nor can we say that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was in Makkah praying for ten years [years] without the Opening of the Book, which is something the intellects do not accept.

The teacher said: I say: some scholars, who reconciled these two views, said: it is both Makkan and Madinan; Jibril descended with it twice, once at Makkah and once at Madina when the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) arrived there, exalting and honouring this surah above others, and for this reason it is called "oft-repeated." And Allah knows best.

Abu Amr Ahmad ibn Abi al-Furat informed us; Abu Musa Imran ibn Musa informed us; Ja'far ibn Muhammad ibn Sawwar narrated to us; Ahmad ibn Nasr informed us; Sa'id ibn Mansur informed us; Salam narrated to us from Zayd al-Ammi, from Ibn Sirin, from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "The Opening of the Book is a cure from poison." [al-Jami' al-Saghir: 2/207] [9]

Abu al-Hasan Muhammad ibn al-Qasim ibn Ahmad narrated to us; Abu Ishaq Ibrahim ibn Muhammad ibn Ayyub narrated to us; Abu Abd Allah Muhammad ibn Sahib narrated to us; al-Ma'mun ibn Ahmad narrated to us; Ahmad ibn Abd Allah narrated to us; Abu Mu'awiya al-Darir narrated to us from Abu Malik al-Ash'ari, from Ibn Humran, from Hudhayfa ibn al-Yaman, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Indeed, when Allah sends punishment upon a people, a decreed certainty, and a child among them reads in the Book: Al-hamdu lillahi rabbi al-'alamin, Allah the Mighty and Majestic hears it and lifts that punishment from them for forty years." [Kashf al-Khafa': 1/221] [10]

Abu al-Qasim al-Hasan ibn Muhammad narrated to us, saying: Abu Ja'far Muhammad ibn Salih ibn Hani narrated to us; al-Husayn ibn al-Fadl narrated to us; Affan ibn Muslim al-Saffar narrated to us, from al-Rabi' ibn Subayh, from al-Hasan, who said:

Allah the Mighty and Majestic sent down one hundred and four books from heaven, and He deposited their sciences in four: the Torah, the Gospel, the Psalms and the Furqan (the Criterion). Then He deposited the sciences of these four in the Furqan, then He deposited the sciences of the Qur'an in the detailed (mufassal) portion, then He deposited the sciences of the mufassal in the Opening of the Book. Whoever knows its tafsir is as one who knows the tafsir of all the books of Allah that were revealed, and whoever recites it is as one who has recited the Torah, the Gospel, the Psalms and the Furqan.

[On the Virtue of the Basmala]

Abu Abd Allah Muhammad ibn Ali narrated to us; Ahmad ibn Sa'id narrated to us; Ja'far ibn Muhammad ibn Salih narrated to us; and Muhammad ibn al-Qasim al-Farisi narrated to us; Abu Muhammad Abd Allah ibn Ahmad al-Shaybani narrated to us; Ahmad ibn Kamil ibn Khalaf informed us; Ali ibn Hammad ibn al-Sakan narrated to us; Ahmad ibn Abd Allah al-Harawi informed us; Hisam ibn Sulayman al-Makhzumi, from Abu Malika, from Ibn Abbas (may Allah be pleased with him), who said: I heard the Prophet (ﷺ) say: "The best of people and the best of those who walk upon the new earth are the teachers. Whenever religion wears out, they renew it. Give them [their wages], and do not hire them, lest you burden them. For when a teacher says to a child: Say: In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful, and the child says: In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful, Allah writes acquittal for the child, acquittal for his two parents, and acquittal for the teacher from the Fire." [Tafsir al-Qurtubi: 1/336] [11]

Abu al-Hasan ibn Abi al-Fadl al-Mawla informed us; Abu Ali al-Isfara'ini al-Hafiz informed us; Ibn al-Hasan al-Basri narrated to us; Muhammad ibn Marwan Abu Ja'far narrated to us; my father narrated to us; Umar ibn Dharr narrated to us, from Ata', from Jabir, who said: "When In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful was revealed, the clouds fled to the east, the winds became still, the sea was stirred, the animals pricked up their ears, the devils were pelted from the sky, and Allah swore by His might that whatever His name is mentioned over will be healed, and whatever His name is mentioned over will be blessed, and whoever recites In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful will enter Paradise." [Tafsir Ibn Kathir: 1/19, with variation.]

al-Hasan ibn Muhammad ibn al-Hasan informed us; Muhammad ibn Muhammad ibn al-Hasan narrated to us; al-Hasan ibn Ali ibn Nasr informed us; Abd Allah ibn Hashim narrated to us; Waki' ibn al-Jarrah informed us, from al-A'mash, from Abu Wa'il, from Abd Allah ibn Mas'ud, who said: "Whoever wishes that Allah save him from the nineteen guardians of Hell, let him recite In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful, for it has nineteen letters, so that Allah will make for him, for each letter of it, a shield from each one." [Tafsir Ibn Kathir: 1/19.] [12]

(Tafsir, and with Allah is success:)

His saying: In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful. Know that this ba' (ب) is extra (za'ida), and it is called the ba' of tadmin (inclusion) or the ba' of ilsaq (attachment), as in your saying: "I wrote with the pen," so the writing is attached to the pen. It is always kasra (vowelled with i), and the reason is that the ba' is a deficient letter that is inclined (mumal). Inclination is one of the indications of kasra. Sibawayh said: "Since the ba' has no function except kasra, it was given kasra."

Al-Mubarrad said: the reason for its kasra is returning it to its origin. Do you not see that when you speak about yourself you say "bi-bayt," so you return it to the ya', and the ya' is a sister of kasra, just as the waw is a sister of damma and the alif is a sister of fatha. It governs what follows it, and therefore the mim of the noun is kasra.

Here it was lengthened and likened to the alif and lam, because they did not wish to begin the Book of Allah except with a magnified and honoured letter. Said by al-Qaysi.

He said: Umar ibn Abd al-Aziz (may Allah have mercy on him) used to say to his scribes: "Lengthen the ba', show the sin clearly, separate them, and round the mim, in glorification of the words of Allah the Most High."

And Abu ... [blank in the manuscript] ... Khalid ibn Yazid al-Muradi said: the reason for it is the omission of the alif from the noun, so when they omitted the alif, they transferred the length of the alif to the ba' to indicate that the alif had been dropped from it. Do you not see that when they wrote iqra' bi-ismi rabbika [Surat al-Alaq: 1] with the alif, they returned the ba' to its form? They only omitted the alif from "ism" here because it frequently recurs on the tongues, acting upon lightness; and since its like does not frequently recur, they kept the alif with them.

In the speech there is an implied and abbreviated element; its estimate is: "Say," or "Begin with the name of Allah."

Adam said: the ism here is superfluous (silah), its sense being: "By Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful is He." They cited the verse of Labid:

"My two daughters wished that their father would live until the year's end, and then: 'the peace be upon you both.' Whoever weeps a full year has excused himself." [Sharh al-Radi 'ala al-Kafiya: 2/242] [Al-Sihah: 2/738]

That is, "then the peace be upon you both."

Its meaning: by Allah the existent things came into being, and by Him the created things stand. They inserted ism so that there would be a distinction between the one who seeks blessing and that by which blessing is sought. As for the meaning of ism, it is the named (al-musamma), the reality of the existent, the essence, the self, the person and the name of a thing; all of these convey one meaning. The proof that the name is the same as the named is His saying, may He be exalted: "Indeed We give you good news of a boy whose name is Yahya" [Surat Maryam: 7]. He informed that his name is Yahya, then He called the name and addressed it, saying: "O Yahya" [Surat Maryam: 13]. So Yahya is the name, and the name is Yahya.

And His saying: "You worship besides Him only names which you have named" [Surat Yusuf: 48], and He meant the worshipped persons, since they used to worship the named ones.

And His saying: "Glorify the name of your Lord, the Most High" [al-A'la: 1], and "Blessed is the name of your Lord" [al-Rahman: 78].

And his saying (ﷺ): "Let Mudar strike the servants of Allah until no name is worshipped but Him" [Majma' al-Zawa'id: 7/313] [13], meaning: until He alone is not worshipped.

Then it is said: we consider the tasmiya (naming) to be ism, and its use in naming is more well known and more frequent than its use for the named; perhaps ism is more well known. Its plural is asma', like qinw and aqnā', and hinw and ahnā'; the waw was dropped due to heaviness, the vowel of the waw was transferred to the mim so the mim became inflected, the sukun of the mim was transferred to the sin so it became quiescent, then a hamzated alif was added because the sin is quiescent, for the sake of beginning. The diminutive and conjugation indicate this, as one says: sumayy and sumayya, because whatever drops out in diminutive and conjugation is not original. Its derivation is from (sama), (yasmu), as if the one described as non-existent, as long as he is non-existent, is in a degree from which he rises when he exists, and by the degree of his existence he rises above the degree of his non-existence. The ism, which is the expression and naming for the one informed about and the attribute for the one described, the origin of ṣifa is the appearance and emergence of a thing. And Allah knows best.

As for what has been reported in its detailed explanation, it is abundant; I have mentioned most of its sayings in hadith and narrative.

Abu al-Qasim ibn Muhammad ibn al-Hasan, the exegete, informed us; Abu al-Tayyib Muhammad ibn Ahmad ibn Hamdun al-Mudhakkir narrated to us; Abu Bakr Muhammad ibn Hamdun ibn Khalid ibn Yazid informed us; Ahmad ibn Hisham al-Antaki narrated to us; al-Hakam ibn Nafi' narrated to us from Isma'il ibn Abbas, from Isma'il, from Yahya, from Abu Malika, from Mas'ud ibn Atiyya al-Awfi, from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Indeed, Isa ibn Maryam his mother entrusted to the kuttab (Qur'anic school) to learn. His teacher said to him: Say [in the source: write], 'In the name of Allah.' Isa said: 'And what is the name of Allah?' The teacher said to him: 'I do not know.' He said: 'The ba': the splendour (bahaʾ) of Allah; the sin: the radiance (sana') of Allah; the mim: the kingdom (mamlaka) of Allah.'" [Jami' al-Bayan of al-Tabari: 1/81] [14]

I heard Abu al-Qasim al-Hasan ibn Muhammad say: I heard Abu Ishaq ibn Maytham ibn Muhammad ibn Yazid al-Nasafi say in Marw: I heard Abu Abd Allah, the in-law of Abu Bakr al-Warraq, say: I heard Abu Bakr Muhammad ibn Umar al-Warraq say concerning "In the name of Allah": it is a garden from the gardens of Paradise, and each letter of it has its own explanation.

The ba' has six aspects:

Creator (bari') of His creation from the Throne to the earth, by the clarification of His saying: "Indeed He is the Good (al-barr), the Merciful" [Surat al-Tur: 28].

Seeing (basir) of His servants from the Throne to the earth; its clarification: "Indeed He is Seeing of everything" [Surat al-Mulk: 19].

Extender (basit) of provision from the Throne to the earth; its clarification: "Allah extends provision to whom He wills and restricts" [Surat al-Ra'd: 26].

And Abiding (baqi) after the annihilation of His creation, from the Throne to the earth; its clarification: "Everyone upon it is perishing, and there remains the Face of your Lord, Owner of Majesty and Honour" [Surat al-Rahman: 26].

Raiser (ba'ith) of creation after death for reward and punishment; its clarification: "And that Allah will raise those in the graves" [Surat al-Hajj: 7].

Good (barr) to the believers from the Throne to the earth; its clarification is His saying: "Indeed He is the Good, the Merciful" [Surat al-Tur: 28].

The sin has five aspects:

Hearing (sami') of the voices of His creation from the Throne to the earth; its clarification is His saying, may He be exalted: "Or do they think that We do not hear their secret and their private talk? Yes, and Our messengers are with them, writing" [Surat al-Zukhruf: 80].

Master (sayyid) whose lordship has reached the highest, from the Throne to the earth; its clarification: "Allah, the Eternal Refuge" [Surat al-Ikhlas: 2].

Swift in reckoning with His creation, from the Throne to the earth; its clarification: "And Allah is swift in reckoning" [Surat al-Baqara: 202].

Safe (salim), sparing His creation from His injustice, from the Throne to the earth; its clarification: "the Peace, the Giver of security" [Surat al-Hashr: 23].

Forgiver of the sins of His servants, from the Throne to the earth; its clarification is His saying: "Forgiver of sin and Acceptor of repentance" [Surat Ghafir: 3].

The mim has twelve aspects:

King (malik) of creation from the Throne to the earth; its clarification: "the King, the Holy" [Surat al-Hashr: 23].

Owner (malik) of His creation from the Throne to the earth; its clarification: "Say: O Allah, Owner of sovereignty" [Surat Al 'Imran: 26].

Bestower (mannan) upon His creation from the Throne to the earth; its clarification: "Rather, Allah bestows favour upon you" [Surat al-Hujurat: 17].

Glorious (majid) over His creation from the Throne to the earth; its clarification: "Owner of the Glorious Throne" [Surat al-Buruj: 15].

Securer (mu'min), who gave security to His creation from the Throne to the earth; its clarification is His saying: "and He gave them security from fear" [Surat Quraysh: 4].

Guardian (muhaymin), who oversees His creation from the Throne to the earth; its clarification: "the Believer, the Guardian" [Surat al-Hashr: 23].

Omnipotent (muqtadir) over His creation from the Throne to the earth; its clarification: "in a seat of truth, in the presence of a Sovereign, Omnipotent" [Surat al-Qamar: 55].

Sustainer (muqit) over His creation from the Throne to the earth; its clarification: "And Allah is ever Sustainer over all things" [Surat al-Nisa': 85].

Honourer (mutakarrim) over His creation from the Throne to the earth; its clarification: "And We have honoured the children of Adam" [Surat al-Isra': 70].

Bounteous (mun'im) over His creation from the Throne to the earth; its clarification is His saying: "And He has completed upon you His favours, apparent and hidden" [Surat Luqman: 20].

Gracious (mutafaddil) over His creation from the Throne to the earth; its clarification: "But Allah is full of bounty to the worlds" [Surat al-Baqara: 251].

Fashioner (musawwir) of His creation from the Throne to the earth; its clarification: "the Creator, the Originator, the Fashioner" [Surat al-Hashr: 24].

And the people of realities (ahl al-haqa'iq) said: [blank in the manuscript] ... In "In the name of Allah" is seeking blessing and sanctification, and urging people to begin their speech and actions with "In the name of Allah," since Allah the Mighty and Majestic began His Book with it.

And Allah knows best.

Commentary of al-Tha'alibi (al-Jawahir al-Hisan) on surah 1, verse 1 (part 2 of 3):

Allah. Know that the origin of this word (ilah, "god") is, according to the people of Kufa, that the definite article (al-) was added to it to magnify and exalt it, as it became the name of Allah, so it became al-ilah. The hamza was then dropped because of the difficulty of its frequent use on the tongues, and its quality was transferred to the lam of magnification, so two lams met and the first was assimilated into the second, and they said Allah.

The people of Basra said: its origin is lah, to which the definite article was added, and they said Allah. They recited:

Like the oath of Abu Rabah's sons... which the great gods hear.
[al-Sihah: 67/2248.]

So he (the poet) kept it in its original form.

Some of them said: the definite article was added in place of the dropped hamza in ilah, so the two (al- and the lam) became attached to the word just as that hamza would have been if it had remained as the original. This is why the vocative particles that precede definite nouns were not used with it; they did not say "ya ayyuha Allah."

The objections of the interpreters regarding this name are based on these two opinions [blank in the manuscript] ... there. They differed about it. Al-Khalil ibn Ahmad and a group said: Allah is a proper name, placed (for God), not derived in any way; had it been derived from an attribute, it would have been applied to others who possess that attribute or part of it. Allah says: "Do you know anyone worthy of His name?" (Maryam 19:65).

Allah is a name placed for the Exalted, which no one shares with Him. Allah says: "Do you know anyone worthy of His name?" That is, every name shared between Him and others is so in reality for Him and metaphorically for others, except this name, which is specific to Him, because it contains the meaning of lordship, and all meanings fall under it. Do you not see that if you remove the alif from it, what remains is lillah; if you remove the first lam from lillah, what remains is lahu; and if you remove the lam from lahu, what remains is huwa.

They said: when this name is applied to other than God, it is said only with an added element, as one says "lah of such-and-such" (a god of so-and-so), or it is negated, saying "la-llah," as Allah says, reporting about the people of Moses, peace be upon him: "Make for us a god as they have gods" (al-A'raf 7:138). As for "Allah" and "al-ilah," they are specific to Allah the Exalted.

Some people said: its origin is laha in Syriac, because at the end of their names there is an extended vowel, as they say for "spirit" ruha, for "holy" qudsa, for "Messiah" masiha, for "son" bna. When they dropped the extended vowel, lah remained, and the Arabs arabized it and adopted it.

It has no derivation, but most scholars hold that it is derived, and they differed about its derivation. Al-Nadr ibn Isma'il said: it is from ta'allah, which means asceticism and worship. Ru'ba said:

By the god of the beautiful women... they glorified and sought forgiveness from my worship (ta'alluhi).

It is said: allaha ilahatan, as one says 'abada 'ibadatan (he worshipped with worship). Ibn 'Abbas recited "wa yadhraka wa ilahataka" (al-A'raf 7:127), meaning your worship, so its meaning is your worship of the one who is truly worthy of worship.

Some said it is from al-ilah, which is reliance. One says: alahtu ila fulan, ya'lahu ilahan, meaning I sought refuge with him and relied on him. A poet said:

I turned to her while the riding camels stood still.

Its meaning is that creatures seek refuge and entreat Him in calamities and needs, so He gives them refuge (yu'alluhum), that is, He protects them, and so He is named ilah, as one says imam for that which is followed, and lihaf, rida', izar and kisa' for the garment with which one wraps oneself. This is the meaning of the words of Ibn 'Abbas and al-Dahhak.

Abu 'Amr ibn al-'Ala said: it is from alaha fi al-shay' (to be bewildered) when one is perplexed about something and does not find guidance to it; this comes from al-walah, which is bewilderment. Zuhayr said:

... [blank in the manuscript] ... the eye wanders in its middle, lightly.

And al-Akhtal said:

We divided the land into two halves, one half for us, and we hoped that the other would be ours too, ninety thousand (acres), the eye wanders in its middle; when the eye of the one who has a view sees it, it weeps.

Its meaning is that intellects are bewildered about the reality of His attributes and greatness and the encompassing of His manner, so He is an ilah, as the written is called kitab and the counted is called hisab.

Al-Mubarrad said: it is from the Arabs' saying alahtu ila fulan, meaning I found rest in him. A poet said:

I found rest in her while the calamities were many.

As if creatures find rest in Him and are reassured by His remembrance, as Allah says: "Surely in the remembrance of Allah do hearts find rest" (al-Ra'd 13:28).

I heard Abu al-Qasim al-Hasan say: I heard Abu al-Hasan 'Ali ibn 'Abd al-Rahim al-Qannad say: its origin is from al-walah, which is the loss of reason from the absence of someone dear to you. Its origin is ali (with a hamza), and the alif was replaced by a waw, so it became al-walah, like ishash and washash, and wakaf and ikaf, and arrakhtu al-kitab and warrakhtuhu, and wuqqitat and uqqitat. Al-Kumayt said:

My soul, longing for them, became bewildered, and bewilderment came between it and the taste of food.

So He was named by this because hearts are bewildered by love for Him and tremble and yearn at His remembrance.

It is said: its meaning is "hidden," because when the Arabs recognize something and then it is hidden from their sight, they call it ilah. He said: the bride became veiled (lahat al-'arusu) when she was hidden.

The poet said:

She was veiled, and on no day was she known to come out; would that she had come out until we saw her.

And Allah the Exalted is manifest through lordship [through proofs and signs], and is hidden in His manner from imaginings.

It is said: its meaning is "the exalted," from "lah," meaning he rose high.

It has also been said: it is from "ilaha" (the Exalted), as the poet said:

We came in the afternoon from the lush land (la'ba') in haste, and hastened the vexation lest it return.

It has been said: it is taken from the saying of the Arabs, alaha bi al-makan, when one dwells in a place. A poet said:

We dwelt in a house whose traces are not clear, as if its remnants were a tattoo on the hand.

So its meaning is: the Enduring, the Established, the Everlasting.

Some people said: [that which is said] (the manuscript has this word) His essence, and it is His power to subdue.

Al-Harith ibn Asad al-Muhasibi, Abu 'Abd Allah al-Baghdadi, said: Allah is from "allahahum," meaning He made them need Him, so the servants are in need of their Creator, that is, they are dependent on Him for benefit and harm, like the bewildered, distressed, overpowered one.

Shahr ibn Hawshab said: Allah is the Creator of every thing. Abu Bakr al-Warraq said: He is...

Some emphasized the lam in His saying "Allah" until they pressed the tongue against the palate, because of the grandeur of His mention, and so that it would be distinguished at the beginning of mentioning Him, and He is the Lord.

Al-Rahman al-Rahim. Some said: both have one meaning, like nadman and nadim, and salman and salim, and hawwan and hawwin. Their meaning is: possessor of mercy. Mercy is God's will for good for His people, and on this view it is an attribute of essence. It has also been said: it is abstaining from punishing one who deserves punishment and doing good to one who does not deserve it; on this view it is an attribute of action. The two are combined for breadth, as the Arabs say jad majd. Tarafa said:

Why do I see myself and my cousin Malik... when I approach him he recedes from me and departs.

Another said:

And he found her words to be lies and falsehood.

Others distinguished between them. Some said: al-Rahman is on the pattern fa'lan, which is used only for intensive meaning, as in your saying ghadban (very angry) for one filled with anger, and sakran for one overcome by drink. So the meaning of al-Rahman is: the One whose mercy encompasses everything.

Some said: al-Rahman is the one who bestows kindness on all His creatures, believers and disbelievers, righteous and wicked, by creating and providing for them. Allah says: "My mercy encompasses everything" (al-A'raf 7:156). And al-Rahim is for the believers specifically, through guidance and success in this world, and Paradise and seeing Him in the Hereafter. Allah says: "And He is ever merciful to the believers" (al-Ahzab 33:43).

So al-Rahman is specific in wording and general in meaning, and al-Rahim is general in wording and specific in meaning. Al-Rahman is specific in that it is not permitted for anyone to be named by it except Allah the Exalted, and general in that it includes all existents through creation, provision, benefit and removal of harm. Al-Rahim is general in that created beings share in being named by it, and specific in meaning because it returns to kindness and success. This is the view of Ja'far ibn Muhammad al-Sadiq, may Allah be pleased with him.

Al-Rahman is a name specific in its attribute and general in its effect, and al-Rahim is a general name with a specific attribute. Ibn 'Abbas said: they are two tender names, one more tender than the other.

Abu al-Qasim al-Hasan ibn Muhammad the exegete informed us: Abu 'Abd Allah Muhammad ibn Yusuf al-Daqqaq told us: al-Hasan ibn Muhammad ibn Jabir told us: 'Abd Allah ibn Hashim told us: Waki' informed us, from Sufyan, from Mansur, from Mujahid, who said: "Al-Rahman" is toward the people of this world, and "al-Rahim" toward the people of the Hereafter.

And it is reported in supplication: "O Rahman of this world and Rahim of the Hereafter."

Al-Dahhak said: al-Rahman is toward the people of heaven, when He caused them to dwell in the heavens, girded them with obedience, kept them from calamities, and cut off from them food and pleasures. Al-Rahim is toward the people of earth, when He sent messengers to them and sent down books upon them, and gave them excuse in counsel, and turned away from them afflictions.

'Ikrimah said: al-Rahman by one mercy, and al-Rahim by a hundred mercies. This meaning he took from the saying of the Prophet ﷺ which Abu al-Qasim al-Hasan ibn Muhammad al-Nisaburi told us: Abu Ishaq Ibrahim ibn Muhammad ibn Yazid al-Nasafi told us in Marw: Abu Hurayrah and Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Shardah al-Kushi told us: Jarud ibn Mu'adh told us: 'Umayr ibn Marwan informed us, from 'Abd al-Malik Abu Sulayman, from 'Ata', from Abu Hurayrah, who said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Allah the Exalted has one hundred mercies; He sent down one of them to the earth and divided it among His creatures, and by it they show compassion to one another and show mercy to one another. He held back ninety-nine for Himself, to show mercy to His servants on the Day of Resurrection." [Sahih Muslim: 8/96; Sunan Ibn Majah: 2/1435, with variation.] [15]

In another narration: "Allah the Exalted will join this to that, and complete them into one hundred on the Day of Resurrection, and by them He will show mercy to His servants." [al-Mustadrak: 4/248, with variation.] [16]

Ibn al-Mubarak said: "Al-Rahman: the One who gives when asked; al-Rahim: the One who becomes angry when not asked." What indicates this is what Abu al-Qasim the exegete told us: Abu Yusuf Rafi' ibn 'Abd Allah told us in Marw al-Rudh: Khalaf ibn Musa told us: Mahmud ibn Khadash told us: Harun ibn Mu'awiyah told us: Abu al-Malj, and he is not al-Raqqi, told us, from Abu Salih, from Abu Hurayrah, from the Prophet ﷺ that he said: "Whoever does not ask Allah, Allah becomes angry with him." [Fath al-Bari: 11/79.] A poet versified it, saying:

Allah becomes angry if you leave off asking Him, and the son of Adam becomes angry when he is asked.

[Tafsir al-Qurtubi: 5/164.] [17]

I heard al-Hasan ibn Muhammad say: I heard Ibrahim ibn Muhammad al-Nasafi say: I heard Abu 'Abd Allah, who was the brother-in-law of Abu Bakr al-Warraq, say: I heard Abu Bakr Muhammad ibn 'Umar al-Warraq say: "Al-Rahman: with blessings, which is what is given and bestowed; al-Rahim: with favors, which is what is withheld and withdrawn."

Muhammad ibn 'Ali al-Mazidi said: al-Rahman is by rescuing from the Fire, and its proof is His saying: "And you were on the brink of a pit of fire, and He rescued you from it" (Al 'Imran 3:103). And al-Rahim is by admitting them into the gardens, its proof being: "Enter them in peace, secure" (al-Hijr 15:46).

Al-Muhasibi said: "Al-Rahman: by the mercy of souls; al-Rahim: by the mercy of hearts."

Al-Sarri ibn Mughallis said: "Al-Rahman: by removing distresses; al-Rahim: by forgiving sins."

'Abd Allah ibn al-Jarrah said: "Al-Rahman: by ... [blank in the manuscript] ... the path; al-Rahim: by protection and success."

Mutahhar ibn al-Warraq said: "Al-Rahman: by forgiving evil deeds, however great they are; al-Rahim: by accepting acts of obedience, however small they are." [blank in the manuscript; what we have mentioned is the apparent reading.]

Yahya ibn Mu'adh al-Razi said: "Al-Rahman: by the interests of their livelihood; al-Rahim: by the interests of their final return."

Al-Husayn ibn al-Fadl said: "Al-Rahman is the One who has mercy on the servant by removing harm and averting evil; al-Rahim is the One who is tender, and perhaps is not able to remove it."

Abu Bakr al-Warraq also said: "Al-Rahman: toward whoever denies Him; al-Rahim: toward whoever affirms His oneness; al-Rahman: toward whoever disbelieves; al-Rahim: toward whoever is grateful; al-Rahman: toward whoever claims rivals for Him; al-Rahim: toward whoever declares Him one."

Whether the basmala is part of al-Fatiha or not.

People differed over whether the basmala is part of al-Fatiha. The reciters of Medina, Basra and Kufa said: it is an opening for seeking blessing and blessing through mentioning Him, and it is not part of al-Fatiha nor of any other surah, and its recitation is not obligatory, and the sixth verse is His saying: "those upon whom You have bestowed favor" (al-Fatiha 1:7). This is the view of Malik ibn Anas, al-Awza'i and Abu Hanifa, may Allah have mercy on them, and they narrated it from Abu Hurayrah.

Abu al-Qasim al-Husayn ibn Muhammad ibn al-Hasan al-Nisaburi informed us: Abu al-Hasan Muhammad ibn al-Hasan al-Kabuli told us: 'Ali ibn 'Abd al-'Aziz al-Hilli informed us: Abu 'Ubayd al-Qasim ibn Salam al-Baghdadi told us: al-Hajjaj told us, from Abu Sa'id al-Hudhali, from ... [blank in the manuscript] ... from Abu Hurayrah, who said: "Those upon whom You have bestowed favor" is the sixth verse. A group claimed that it is a verse of the Mother of the Qur'an, and in the rest of the surahs there is a separation, so it is not here that it must be recited.

[Others said: it is a verse of al-Fatiha.] [Unreadable text; the apparent reading is what we have recorded.] They narrated this from Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab, and the reciters of Mecca and Kufa and most reciters of the Hijaz said so as well, and they did not count "those upon whom You have bestowed favor" as a verse.

Al-Shafi'i, al-Sha'bi, and the opinion of 'Abd Allah (ibn Mas'ud) said that it was revealed as the first verse of al-Fatiha, and that it is a verse of every surah except al-Tawba. The evidence for this is the Book and the Sunnah. As for the Book: I heard Abu 'Uthman ibn Abi Bakr al-Za'farani say: I heard my father say: I heard Abu Bakr Muhammad ibn Ahmad ibn Musa say: I heard al-Hasan ibn al-Mufaddal say: I saw the people ... [blank in the manuscript] ... in Surah al-Naml that "In the name of Allah, the Compassionate, the Merciful" is in it as part of the Qur'an. I found it in its script, even though it is repeated in the Qur'an, and we know its places in it. Indeed, even "Then which of the favors of your Lord will you deny?" (al-Rahman 55:13) and "Woe that Day to the deniers" (al-Mursalat 77:15), since they are in the Qur'an, their repetitions are from the Qur'an.

It has reached us that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ at the beginning of the matter wrote, in the script of Quraysh, "In Your name, O Allah," until it was revealed: "And he said, 'Embark therein; in the name of Allah is its course and its anchorage'" (Hud 11:41), so he wrote, "In the name of Allah," until it was revealed: "Say: Call upon Allah or call upon al-Rahman" (al-Isra' 17:110), so he wrote, "In the name of Allah, al-Rahman," until it was revealed: "Indeed it is from Solomon, and indeed it is: In the name of Allah, the Compassionate, the Merciful" (al-Naml 27:30), so he wrote the like of it. When it was ... this ... [blank in the manuscript] ... from it. Then the Prophet ﷺ took pride in this verse, and he had the right to do so.

'Abd Allah ibn Hamid ibn Muhammad al-Warraq told us: Abu Bakr Ahmad ibn Ishaq al-Faqih informed us: Muhammad ibn Yahya ibn Sahl told us: Adam ibn Abi Iyas told us: Salamah ibn al-Ahmar told us, from Yazid ibn Abi Khalid, from 'Abd al-Karim ibn Umayyah, from Abu Burdah, from his father, who said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Shall I not inform you of a verse that was not revealed to anyone after Solomon son of David except me?" I said: "Yes." He said: "With what do you begin when you begin the Qur'an?" I said: "In the name of Allah, the Compassionate, the Merciful." He said: "It is, it is." [Majma' al-Zawa'id: 2/109, with variation.] [18]

In this hadith there is evidence that the basmala is a complete verse of al-Fatiha and of the openings of the surahs, because the Prophet ﷺ pronounced the whole verse, whereas the one in Surah al-Naml is not a verse by itself but only part of a verse. And success is from Allah.

As for the reports related about it,

Commentary of al-Tha'alibi (al-Jawahir al-Hisan) on surah 1, verse 1 (part 3 of 3):

Abu al-Qasim al-Sadusi informed us: Abu Zakariyya Yahya ibn Muhammad ibn Abd Allah al-Anbari narrated to us: Ibrahim ibn Ishaq al-Anmati narrated to us: Ya'qub ibn Ibrahim al-Dawraqi narrated to us: Abu Sufyan al-Mu'mari narrated to us, from Ibrahim ibn Yazid, who said: I said to Amr ibn Dinar: "Al-Fadl al-Raqashi claims that ﴿In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful﴾ is not part of the Qur'an?" He said: "Glory be to God! How audacious this man is! I heard Sa'id ibn Jubayr say: I heard Ibn Abbas say: When the Messenger of God (ﷺ) would receive a verse, ﴿In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful﴾, he would know that the surah had ended and another was beginning."

Al-Hasan ibn Muhammad narrated to us: Abu al-Hasan Isa ibn Zayd al-Aqili narrated to us: Abu Muhammad Isma'il ibn Isa al-Wasiti narrated to us: Abd Allah ibn Nafi' narrated to us, from Jahm ibn Uthman, from Ja'far ibn Muhammad, from his father, from Jabir ibn Abd Allah, that the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "How do you recite when you stand up for prayer?" He said: "I say: ﴿All praise is due to God, Lord of the worlds﴾." He said: "Say: ﴿In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful﴾." [19] [(Source: Tarikh Jurjan: 491.)]

Al-Hasan ibn Muhammad narrated to us, Abu al-Husayn informed us [Blank in the manuscript.] ..., Ali ibn Abd al-Aziz narrated to us, Abu Ubayd narrated to us, Umar ibn Harun al-Balkhi narrated to us, from Abu Salih, from Abu Malika, from Maslama, that the Messenger of God (ﷺ) used to recite: ﴿In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful﴾ ﴿All praise is due to God, Lord of the worlds﴾ ﴿the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful﴾ ﴿Master of the Day of Judgement﴾, meaning he would separate them verse by verse, until he counted seven verses, as the Bedouins count.

Abu al-Hasan Muhammad ibn Ahmad informed us: Abu Ahmad Abd Allah ibn Adi, the hafiz (memorizer of hadith), narrated to us: Muhammad ibn Ja'far narrated to us: Isma'il ibn Abi Uways narrated to us: al-Husayn ibn Abd Allah narrated to us, from his father, from his grandfather, from Ali ibn Abi Talib (may God honour his face), that when he began a surah in prayer he would recite ﴿In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful﴾, and he would say: "Whoever abandons its recitation has fallen short." And he would say: "It is the completion of the seven oft-repeated [verses] and the Great Qur'an."

Al-Husayn ibn Muhammad ibn Ja'far informed us: Abu al-Abbas al-Asamm narrated to us: Ahmad ibn Abd al-Jabbar al-Attaridi narrated to us: Ja'far ibn Hayyan narrated to us, from Abd al-Malik ibn Jurayj, from his father, from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, from Ibn Abbas, concerning His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And We have certainly given you seven of the oft-repeated [verses]﴾ [Surat al-Hijr: 87]. He said: "It is the Opening of the Book (al-Fatiha)."

It was said to Ibn Abbas: "Where is the seventh?" He said: "﴿In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful﴾," and he counted [them] on his fingers, then said: "I have shown them to you, and I do not find in them your command [to omit it]."

[Muhammad ibn al-Husayn] informed us: Abd Allah ibn Muhammad ibn Muslim narrated to us: Yazid ibn Sinan narrated to us: Abu Bakr al-Hanafi narrated to us: Nuh ibn Abi Bilal narrated to us, who said: I heard al-Maqbari, from Abu Hurayra, that he said:
"When you recite Umm al-Qur'an (the Mother of the Qur'an), do not neglect ﴿In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful﴾, for it is one of its verses, and it is the seven oft-repeated [verses]."

Abu al-Qasim al-Hasan ibn Muhammad ibn Habib informed us: Abu Zakariyya Yahya ibn Muhammad ibn Abd Allah al-Anbari informed us: Ja'far ibn Ahmad ibn Nasr al-Hafiz narrated to us: Ahmad ibn Nasr narrated to us: Adam ibn Iyas narrated to us, from Abu Sam'an, from al-Ala, from his father, from Abu Hurayra, that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "God says: I have divided the prayer between Me and My servant into two halves. When the servant says: ﴿In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful﴾, God says: My servant has glorified Me. When the servant says: ﴿All praise is due to God, Lord of the worlds﴾, God says: My servant has praised Me. When he says: ﴿the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful﴾, He says: My servant has extolled Me. When he says: ﴿Master of the Day of Judgement﴾, God says: My servant has entrusted his affair to Me. When he says: ﴿You alone we worship, and You alone we ask for help﴾, God says: This is between Me and My servant. When he says: ﴿Guide us to the straight path﴾, God says: This is for My servant, and My servant shall have what he asks." [20] [(Source: al-Sunan al-Kubra: 1/316; Ahkam al-Qur'an: 1/8; Tafsir Ibn Kathir: 1/12, with variations.)]

Ali ibn Muhammad ibn al-Hasan al-Muqri informed us: Abu Nasr Ahmad ibn Muhammad al-Qassar informed us: Muhammad ibn Bakr al-Basri narrated to us: Muhammad ibn Ali al-Jawhari narrated to us: [Blank in the manuscript.] ..., Abu Isma'il ibn Yahya narrated to me [Blank in the manuscript.] ..., Sufyan al-Thawri narrated to us, from Muhammad ibn Amr, from Abu Salama, from Abu Hurayra, who said: "I was with the Prophet (ﷺ), and the Prophet (ﷺ) was speaking to his companions, when a man entered and prayed. He began the prayer, sought refuge [in God], then said: ﴿All praise is due to God, Lord of the worlds﴾. The Prophet (ﷺ) heard him and said: 'O man, you have cut your prayer short for yourself. Do you not know that ﴿In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful﴾ is part of the praise? Whoever omits it has omitted a verse, and whoever omits a verse of it has invalidated his prayer.'" [21] [(Source: al-Durr al-Manthur: 1/7, from al-Tha'labi.)] The prayer is not valid except with the Opening of the Book, and whoever omits a verse, his prayer is void.

Abu al-Husayn Ali ibn Muhammad al-Jurjani informed us: Abu Bakr Ahmad ibn Ibrahim al-Isma'ili narrated to us: Abu Bakr Muhammad ibn Umar ibn Hisham narrated to us: Muhammad ibn Yahya informed us: Hakim ibn al-Husayn narrated to us: Sulayman ibn Muslim al-Makki narrated to us, from Nafi', from Abu Malika, from Talha ibn Ubayd Allah, who said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "Whoever omits ﴿In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful﴾ has omitted a verse from the Book of God." [22] [(Source: al-Durr al-Manthur: 1/7.)]

Ali (peace be upon him) counted it among what he counted of Umm al-Kitab (the Mother of the Book).

As for consensus (al-ijma', i.e., scholarly agreement):
Abu Muhammad Abd Allah ibn Hamid al-Warraq informed us: Abu Bakr Ahmad ibn Ishaq al-Dab'i informed us: Abd Allah ibn Muhammad narrated to us: Muhammad ibn Yahya narrated to us: Ali ibn al-Madini narrated to us: Abd al-Wahhab ibn Fulayh narrated to us, from Abd Allah ibn Maymun, from Ubayd ibn Rifa'a, that Mu'awiya ibn Abi Sufyan came to Medina and led the people in a prayer in which he recited aloud. When he recited Umm al-Qur'an and did not recite ﴿In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful﴾, and finished his prayer, the Emigrants and the Helpers called out to him from every direction: "Have you forgotten? Where is ﴿In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful﴾ when you began the Qur'an?" So Mu'awiya repeated it for them and recited ﴿In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful﴾.

Discussion on the basmala as part of the other surahs:
This applies to the Fatiha. As for the other surahs:
Abu al-Qasim al-Habibi informed us: Abu al-Abbas al-Asamm narrated to us: al-Rabi' ibn Sulayman narrated to us: al-Shafi'i informed us: Abd al-Majid ibn Abd al-Aziz informed us, from Ibn Jurayj, from Abd Allah ibn Uthman ibn Khuthaym, that Abu Bakr ibn Hafs ibn Asim said: "Mu'awiya led a prayer in Medina in which he recited aloud. He recited ﴿In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful﴾ for Umm al-Qur'an, and did not recite it for the surah that followed until he finished his prayer. When he gave the salam, the Emigrants called out to him from every place: 'O Mu'awiya, have you stolen from the prayer, or have you forgotten?' So he led them in another prayer and recited [the basmala] for the surah that followed."

[Blank in the manuscript.] ..
The consideration of the verses of the Qur'an: the endings (maqati') of the Qur'anic verses are of two kinds: rhyming similarly (mutaqariba) and rhyming in a patterned way (mutashakila).
The patterned kind is like what is in Surat al-Qamar and al-Rahman and similar [surahs]. The similarly rhyming kind is said to be in Surat Qaf: ﴿Qaf. By the glorious Qur'an! Rather, they wonder that a warner from among themselves has come to them, and the disbelievers say: This is a strange thing﴾ [Surat Qaf: 1-2], and what resembles it. Then we considered His saying: "qablihim" (before them), and it was neither of the patterned kind nor of the similar kind. We found that the endings of the verses of the Qur'an rest on two letters: a mim or a nun, or a sound letter preceded by a kasra, or a waw with a damma before it, or an alif with a fatha before it. We found that their way is other than the arrangement of the Book.
"This, and we have not seen any verse of the Book of God begin without [the basmala]..."
.. He also says: The basmala is not free of [being] either: written to separate the surahs, or at the end of the surahs, or at their beginnings, or that it was written when it was revealed, and where it was not revealed it was not written. If it had been written for separation, it would have been written [in Bara'a]... [Blank in the manuscript.] ... and [so forth]. If it had been written at the beginning, it would have been written in (Bara'a) [Surat al-Tawba]. If it had been written at the end, it would have been written at the end of ﴿Say: I seek refuge in the Lord of mankind﴾ [Surat al-Nas: 1]. When these possibilities were rejected, we knew that it was written where it was revealed, and where it was not revealed it was not written.
He also says: We found that they wrote what was not Qur'an of the verses and the other [markings] in red or green, and they wrote the basmala in black. So we knew that it is Qur'an. And success is from God.

The ruling on reciting the basmala aloud in prayer:
Then reciting it aloud in prayer is a sunna, based on God's saying, exalted is He: ﴿Recite in the name of your Lord﴾ [Surat al-Alaq: 2], [so He commanded] [Blank in the manuscript.] His Messenger to recite the Qur'an with the basmala. And He said: ﴿He has succeeded who purifies himself and remembers the name of his Lord and prays﴾ [Surat al-Ala: 14-15]. So He made success obligatory for whoever prays with the basmala.

Abu al-Qasim [al-Hasan ibn Muhammad ibn Ja'far] informed us: Abu Sakhr Muhammad ibn Malik al-Sa'di narrated to us in Merv: Abd al-Samad ibn al-Fadl al-Amuli narrated to us: Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Yahya ibn Hamza al-Hadrami narrated to us in the Ghouta [of Damascus] [Blank in the manuscript.], who said: "I prayed behind al-Mahdi, Commander of the Faithful, and he recited aloud ﴿In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful﴾. I said: 'What is this recitation, O Commander of the Faithful?' He [said]: My father narrated to me, from his father, from Abd Allah ibn Abbas, that the Prophet (ﷺ) recited ﴿In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful﴾ aloud." I said: "Did you transmit it from him?" He said: "Yes." [(Source: al-Bidaya wa'l-Nihaya: 10/162.)]

Al-Hasan ibn Muhammad ibn Zakariyya al-Anbari narrated to us: Muhammad ibn Abd al-Salam narrated to us: Ishaq ibn Ibrahim narrated to us: Khaythama ibn Sulayman informed us, who said: I heard Layth say: "Ata', Tawus and Mujahid used to recite ﴿In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful﴾ aloud."

Al-Hasan ibn Muhammad narrated to us: Abu Bakr Ahmad ibn Abd al-Rahman al-Marwazi narrated to us: al-Hasan ibn Ali ibn Nusayr al-Tusi narrated to us: Abu Maytham Sahl ibn Muhammad narrated to us: Abu Abd Allah Muhammad ibn Abd Allah al-Khuza'i narrated to us, from Ammar ibn Salama, from Ali ibn Zayd ibn Jud'an, that the Abadila (the four Abdullahs) used to begin the recitation with ﴿In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful﴾, reciting it aloud: Abd Allah ibn Abbas, Abd Allah ibn Umar, Abd Allah ibn al-Zubayr, and Abd Allah ibn Safwan.

Al-Hasan ibn Muhammad narrated to us: Abu Nasr Mansur ibn Abd Allah al-Isfahani narrated to us: Abu al-Qasim al-Iskandarani narrated to us: Abu Ja'far al-Malati narrated to us, from Ali ibn Musa al-Rida, from his father, from Ja'far ibn Muhammad, that he said: "The family of Muhammad agreed on reciting ﴿In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful﴾ aloud, and on making up what they missed of the night prayer during the day, and on speaking the best of words about Abu Bakr and Umar and their companion."

With this same chain he said: al-Sadiq was asked about reciting the basmala aloud, and he said: "The truth is to recite it aloud, and it is the one God, mighty and majestic, mentioned: ﴿And when you mention your Lord alone in the Qur'an, they turn back on their backs in aversion﴾ [Surat al-Isra: 46]."

Al-Hasan narrated to us: Abu Muhammad Abd Allah ibn Muhammad ibn Musa ibn Ka'b al-Adl narrated to us: al-Husayn ibn Ahmad ibn al-Layth narrated to us: Muhammad ibn al-Mu'alla al-Muradi narrated to us: Abu Nu'aym narrated to us, from Khalid ibn Iyas, from Sa'id ibn Abi Sa'id al-Muqri, from Abu Hurayra, who said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "Gabriel came to me and taught me the prayer." [23] [(Source: Kanz al-Ummal: 7/441.)] Then the Messenger of God (ﷺ) stood, said the takbir, and recited ﴿In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful﴾ aloud.

Al-Hasan ibn Muhammad narrated to us: Abu al-Tayyib Muhammad ibn Ahmad ibn Hamdun narrated to us: al-Sharqi narrated to us: Muhammad ibn Yahya narrated to us: Ibn Abi Maryam narrated to us, from Yahya ibn Ayyub and Nafi' ibn Ayyub, who both said: Uqayl narrated to us, from al-Zuhri, who said: "It is part of the sunna of the prayer that you recite ﴿In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful﴾ in the Opening of the Book; [if] he does not recite ﴿In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful﴾, he does not recite the surah." He also said: "The first to abandon ﴿In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful﴾ was Amr ibn Sa'id ibn al-As in Medina."

And the one who holds that the basmala is from the Fatiha, and that it is to be recited aloud in prayer, argues by what:
Abd Allah ibn Hamid informed us: Muhammad ibn al-Husayn ibn al-Hasan ibn al-Khalil al-Nisaburi al-Qattan informed us: Muhammad ibn Ibrahim al-Jurjani narrated to us: Ibrahim ibn Ammar narrated to us, from Sa'id ibn Abi Arouba, from al-Hajjaj ibn al-Hajjaj, from Qatada, from Anas ibn Malik, who said: "I prayed with the Messenger of God (ﷺ), Abu Bakr, Umar and Uthman, and I did not hear any of them recite ﴿In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful﴾."

Abd Allah ibn Hamid informed us: Muhammad ibn Isma'il al-Ammari informed us: Yazid ibn Ahmad ibn Yazid narrated to us: Abu Amr narrated to us: Muhammad ibn Uthman narrated to us: Sa'id ibn Bashir narrated to us, from Qatada, from Anas, that the Prophet (ﷺ), Abu Bakr, Umar and Uthman did not recite aloud, and they recited ﴿In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful﴾ silently.

From this hadith it is known that it did not deny that this verse is part of the surah, but it addressed only the omission of reciting aloud. By his saying "they did not recite aloud" he meant that they did not strain to raise their voices, and he did not mean that they recited it secretly or omitted it altogether.

This is supported by what:

﴿Master of the Day of Judgment﴾ [[Surah al-Fatihah: 4.]].

The reciters (qurra') differed concerning it in ten ways (wujuh, sing. wajh, "mode of recitation").

The first mode: **Maliki** (with an alif and a kasra on the kaf), as a descriptive adjective (na't). This is the recitation of the Prophet (ﷺ), Abu Bakr, Umar, Uthman, Ali, Talha, al-Zubayr, Sa'd, Abd al-Rahman ibn Awf, Ibn Mas'ud, Ubayy ibn Ka'b, Mu'adh ibn Jabal, Ibn Abbas, Abu Dhar, Abu Hurayrah, Anas and Mu'awiya.
