**The difference between Malik and Maliki**

As for the difference between *Maliki* and *Malik*, some people said: they are two dialectal forms with one meaning, like *farihin* and *fari'in*, *hadhirin* and *hadhirin*, *fakihin* and *fakihin*. [gap in the manuscript] Between them. Abu Ubaydah, al-Asma'i, Abu Salim, al-Akhfash and Abu al-Haytham said: *Maliki* is more comprehensive, broader and more praiseworthy. Do you not see that one says: "Allah is the Owner (malik) of the birds, the beasts, the wild animals and everything," and one does not say "Malik of everything," but rather says "Malik of the people"? They said: The owner (malik) of a thing is only the one who possesses it, whereas one may be "malik" of a thing without possessing it, as in the phrase "king of the Arabs, the non-Arabs and the Romans."

They also said: the word *al-malik* combines the verbal and the nominal sense.

Some of them said: in *Maliki* [gap in the manuscript] and *Maliki*.

The Prophet's saying (ﷺ): "Whoever recites the Qur'an, for him there is a good deed for every letter, and each good deed is multiplied tenfold" [[al-Burhan: 1/445.]] [27].

Abu Ubayd said: What we choose is *Malik*, [gap in the manuscript] transmitted from the Prophet (ﷺ) is more firmly established, and more of the people of knowledge have recited it. And it is also more correct in meaning, because of the words of the Exalted: ﴿So exalted is Allah, the True King﴾ [[Surah Ta-Ha: 114.]], and ﴿the King, the Holy﴾ [[Surah al-Hashr: 23.]], and ﴿the King of mankind﴾ [[Surah al-Nas: 2.]], and ﴿Whose is the kingdom today?﴾ [[Surah Ghafir: 16.]]. He did not say, "Whose is the *malik* today?"

*Al-malk* is the verbal noun of *malaka* and others, and *malik* is suitable for both *malik* (owner) and *malik* (sovereign). It is said: "He owns the thing (malaka al-shay'), owning it (yamlikuhu) possession (mulkan), so he is *malik* (owner) and *malik* (possessor)" and: "He possesses it (yamlikuhu) possession (mulkan), so he is *malik* (only)." Both of them, after the people, mean "lord" (rabb), because the Arabs say: "the lord of the house, the slave and the estate," meaning he is its owner, and they do not distinguish between their saying *rabbuha* and *malikuha*...

[gap in the manuscript] said: The owner (al-malik) and the sovereign (al-malik) is the one able to bring entities out of non-existence into existence, and in reality none can bring them out except Allah, the Owner.

The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "There is no sovereign except Allah" [[Majma' al-Zawa'id: 10/44.]] [28].

As for others, they are called *malik* (owner) and *malik* (sovereign) figuratively. The meaning is that he is permitted to dispose of it.

Abd al-Aziz ibn Yahya said: The *malik* (owner) is able through what he owns, independent of it among his kind, its benefits returning to him. The second *malik* is the one in whose hand the thing is, who controls it and disposes of it as he wishes. The Arabs say: "*mallakaka* the camel's halter" [i.e., he put its halter in your hand], "I *malaktu* the dough when I kneaded it," and "*amlakat* the woman *imlakan*" [i.e., she was given in marriage]. The poet said:

"And Gabriel, the trustworthy of Allah, gave her in marriage."

**The meaning of His words "al-Din"**

As for the meaning of His words *Maliki Yawmi al-Din*, Ibn Abbas, al-Suddi and Muqatil said: the judge of the Day of Reckoning. Its evidence is the Exalted's words: ﴿That is the upright religion (al-din al-qayyim)﴾ [[Surah al-Tawbah: 36.]], meaning the upright reckoning.

Al-Dahhak and Qatadah said: *al-Din* is the recompense, meaning the day on which Allah requites the servants for their deeds. Its evidence is His words: ﴿Shall we, indeed, be brought to account?﴾ [[Surah al-Saffat: 53.]], meaning "shall we be tested." Labid said:

"Your harvest one day is what you sowed, and indeed
the young man is requited one day as he himself acted."

Uthman ibn Zayyat said: it is the day of subjugation and domination. The Arabs say: *madan fadan*, meaning "I subdued him and he submitted and was humbled." Al-A'sha said:

"He subdued the Rabab when they hated the *din*,
by a raid and a departure,
Then after the Rabab they submitted, and it was
like the punishment of the consequences of speech."

I heard Abu al-Qasim al-Husayn ibn Muhammad the man of letters say: I heard Abu al-Mudir Muhammad ibn Ahmad ibn Mansur say: I heard Abu Umar, the servant of Tha'lab, say: "A man, when he obeyed, *dana*, and when he disobeyed, *dana*; *dana* when he was mighty, and *kana* when he was humbled; *dana* when he was subdued."

Al-Hasan ibn al-Fadl said: "the day of obedience." Zuhayr said:

"If you should alight in a valley in the Banu Asad
in the *din* of Amr, and Fadak comes between us..."

meaning "in obedience." Everything in which Allah is obeyed is *din*.

Some said: "the day of action." Al-Farra' said: "*din* of a man is his character, his deed and his habit." Al-Muthaqqib al-Abdi said:

"She says, when I push away her hobbled [camel]:
'Is this his *din* forever, and mine?'"

Muhammad ibn Ka'b al-Qurazi said: "the Master of a day on which nothing benefits except *din*." This is from the words of Allah: ﴿The day when neither wealth nor children will benefit, except one who comes to Allah with a sound heart﴾ [[Surah al-Shu'ara': 88–89.]], and His words: ﴿It is not your wealth nor your children that bring you near to Us in position, except those who believe and do righteous work﴾ [[Surah Saba': 37.]].

The Day of Religion (yawm al-Din) was singled out for His being its Owner because possessions on that day are gone [so the Exalted alone is singled out with that] [[Addition to make the text sound.]], and they are void, and ownership belongs exclusively to Him. It was also said: the Day of Religion was singled out for the Owner in it because the kingdom of this world is subsumed in His words: ﴿Lord of the worlds﴾ [[Surah al-Hamd: 2.]]. So He affirmed that He is the Owner of the Hereafter by His words *Maliki Yawmi al-Din*, so that it would be known that sovereignty belongs to Him in both abodes. It was also said: the Day of Religion was singled out for mention to inspire awe and to magnify its matter, as the Exalted said: ﴿The day they will come forth, nothing of them will be hidden from Allah﴾ [[Surah Ghafir: 16.]], although they are never hidden from Allah, Mighty and Majestic, at any time.

The shift from third person to second person is called *talwin* (variation of address). It is said that there is an implied ellipsis here, meaning: say, "*iyyaka*." *Iyya* is a pronoun, but it occurs only in the accusative position, and the *ka* is in the genitive position, since *iyya* is attached to it. It is specifically joined to a pronoun because it is attached to a pronominal noun. Does the poet not say:

"So leave me and Khalid,
I will surely sever the sinew of his heart."

Al-Khalil (ibn Ahmad al-Farahidi) related from the Arabs: "When a man reaches sixty, then *iyyahu* and *iyyakum*."

It is used placed before the verb, as in "*Iyyaka a'nee*" (it is you I mean) and "*Iyyaka as'al*" (it is you I ask). It is not used placed after the verb, except that [Gap in the manuscript] ... at the time of the verb, so one says: "*Ma 'abadtu illa iyyaka*" (I worship none but You) and similar.

Abu Maytham Sahl ibn Muhammad said: *iyyaka* is a detached pronoun (*damir munfasil*). Pronouns are of three types:

A connected pronoun (*damir muttasil*), such as the *ka*, *ha* and *ya* in your saying *akramaka* (he honoured you) and *akramani* (he honoured me). It is so named because it is connected to the verb.

A detached pronoun (*damir munfasil*), such as *iyyaka*, *iyyahu* and *iyyaya*. It is so named because it is separate from the verb.

A hidden pronoun (*damir mustakinn*), like the pronoun in your saying *qa'ada* (he sat) and *qama* (he stood). It is so named because it is hidden in the verb and is not expressed in the wording. It includes the implied subject pronoun, since the verb cannot stand without a subject, whether apparent or hidden.

Abu Zayd said: they are two *ya*'s: the first for attribution (*nisba*) and the second for the vocative, their underlying form being (*ayyu ya*). They were merged, and the hamza was given a kasra because of the sukun of the *ya*.

Abu 'Ubayd said: its origin is *awyaka*, the *waw* was changed into *ya* and they were merged. Its root is from *awa, yu'wi, i'wa'* (to shelter, to take refuge), as if it contained the meaning of cutting off and intending.

Al-Fadl al-Raqashi read *Ayyaka* with an open *alif*, and this is a dialect form.

He did not say *na'buduka* (we worship You) because that would be acceptable in expression, but *iyyaka na'budu* is the more eloquent expression, because when they say "*iyyaka na'budu*" their attention is directed to the worship, not from the worship toward Him. His saying *na'budu* means we affirm His unity (*nuwahhidu*), we sincerely devote (*nukhlisu*), we obey (*nut'i*) and we submit humbly (*nakhdau*). Worship (*'ibada*) is the training of the self to bear hardships in obedience. Its root meaning is submission, yielding, obedience and humility. One says: a *tariq mu'abbad* (a well-trodden path) when it is made smooth and trodden by feet. Tarafa said:

"They race with swift, noble she-camels, and they follow
one hoof after another over a well-trodden path."

And a *ba'ir mu'abbad* (a camel smeared with tar) when it is coated with tar. Tarafa said:

"Until the whole tribe shunned me,
and I was left alone like a tar-smeared camel."

The servant ('abd) is called *'abd* because of his humility and his submission to his master.

*Iyyaka nasta'een*: we seek fulfilment and ask for help in Your worship and in all our affairs. One says *asta'anahu* and *asta'anu bihi* (I asked him for help). Yahya ibn Ri'ab read *nasta'in* with a kasra on the *nun*. Al-Farra' said: Tamim, Qays, Asad and Rabi'a pronounce the prefix vowels of the imperfect with a kasra except the *ya*, so they say *yasta'in* and *nasta'in* and similar, and they open the *ya* because it is the sister of the kasra. Quraysh and Kinana open all of them, and this is the more eloquent and more well-known form.

He repeated *iyyaka* to make it more indicative of sincerity (*ikhlas*), exclusivity (*ikhtisas*) and emphasis, following God's saying, reporting about Moses: ﴿That we may glorify You much and remember You much﴾ (Q 20:33–34). He did not say "that we may glorify You and remember You much."

A poet said:

"And He who made the sun a clear boundary, undisguised,
between the day and the night, distinguishing them."

He did not say "between the day and the night." Another said:

"Between al-Ashajj and Qays the lofty:
bakh bakh for his father and for the son."

Abu Bakr al-Warraq said: *iyyaka na'budu* because You created us, and *iyyaka nasta'een* because You guided us. I heard Abu al-Qasim al-Habibi say: I heard Abu al-Hasan 'Ali ibn 'Abd al-Rahman al-Farran, when he was asked about the verse, say:

*Iyyaka na'budu* because You are the Maker, and *iyyaka nasta'een* because the made has no independence from the Maker. *Iyyaka na'budu* so that You admit us into the gardens, and *iyyaka nasta'een* so that You rescue us from the fires. *Iyyaka na'budu* because we are servants, and *iyyaka nasta'een* because You are the Generous, the Glorious. *Iyyaka na'budu* because You are the Worshipped in truth, and *iyyaka nasta'een* because we are the servants in sure bond.

Commentary of al-Tha'alibi (al-Jawahir al-Hisan) on surah 1, verse 6:

﴿Guide us﴾,

ʿAli ibn Abi Talib (may Allah honor his face) and Ubayy ibn Kaʿb said: "Direct us" (arshadtana).

This is like saying to a man who is eating, "Eat" (kul), to one who is reading, "Read" (iqra'), and to one who is standing, "Stand for me until I return to you," meaning: remain in the state you are in. Al-Suddi and Muqatil said: "Guide us," meaning "Show us the way." It is said: "I guided him to the religion" (hadaytuhu lil-din) and "I guided him to the religion" (hadaytuhu ila al-din), with the verbal noun huda and hidaya. Al-Hasan ibn al-Fadl said: guidance (al-huda) in the Qur'an has two aspects.

The first aspect: guidance as invitation and clarification, as in His saying: ﴿And indeed, you guide to a straight path﴾ [Surah al-Shura 42:52], His saying: ﴿And for every people there is a guide﴾ [Surah al-Ra'd 13:7], and: ﴿As for Thamud, We guided them﴾ [Surah Fussilat 41:17].

The second aspect: guidance as granting success and steadfastness, as in His saying: ﴿He leaves astray whom He wills and guides whom He wills﴾ [Surah al-Nahl 16:93], and His saying: ﴿Indeed, you do not guide whom you like﴾ [Surah al-Qasas 28:56].

And al-Sirat al-Mustaqim (the straight path) is the clear, even road. ʿAmir ibn al-Tufayl said:

"We trampled their land with horses until We left them more humbled than the road."

And Jarir said:

"The Commander of the Believers is on a path that, when the watering-places bend, remains straight."

The difference in the reading of al-Sirat

There are five readings of al-Sirat:
With the sin (s), which is the original form; the road was called sirat because it swallows (yastariṭu) those who pass along it.

Abdullah ibn Hamid informed us, Muhammad ibn Hamdawayh informed us, Mahmud ibn Adam informed us, Sufyan informed us, from Umar, from Thabit, who said: I heard Ibn ʿAbbas recite "al-Sirat" with the sin.

Ibn Kathir also recited it thus, through a chain [of transmission] ... [blank in the manuscript] ... and Yaʿqub through a chain ... [blank in the manuscript] ...

With the sin mixed with the zay sound (ishmam al-sin), which is the narration of Abu Hamdun from al-Kisa'i; and with the zay, which is the narration of Abu Hamdun from Sulaym from Hamza.

With the ishmam of the zay, which is the reading of Hamza in most transmissions, and of al-Kisa'i in the narration of Nahshal and al-Shirazi.

With the sad (ṣ), which is the reading of the rest of the readers.

All of these are eloquent and correct dialects, except that the preferred form is with the sad, because it agrees with the Mushaf, since it is written with a sad in all the copies of the Mushaf; and because its counterpart is with the ta, as both agree in emphasis (al-itbaq) and elevation (al-istiʿla').

The exegetes differed concerning al-Sirat al-Mustaqim.

Abu Muhammad Abdullah ibn Hamid and Abu al-Qasim al-Hasan ibn Muhammad al-Nisaburi informed us, both saying: Abu Muhammad Ahmad ibn Abdullah al-Muzani informed us, Muhammad ibn Abdullah ibn Sulayman informed us, al-Husayn ibn Ali informed us, from Hamza al-Zayyat, from Abu al-Mukhtar al-Ta'i, from [Ibn] the son of the brother of al-Harith al-A'war, from al-Harith, from Ali, who said: I heard the Prophet (ﷺ) [say]: "The straight path is the Book of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic."

Abdullah ibn Hamid informed us, Hamid ibn Muhammad informed us, Muhammad ibn Shadhan al-Jawhari informed us, Zakariyya ibn ʿAdi informed us, from Muqtada, from Mansur, from Abu Wa'il, from Abdullah, who said: "The straight path is the Book of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic."

Abdullah informed us, Abd al-Rahman ibn Muhammad informed us, Layth informed us, Uqba ibn Sulayman informed us, al-Husayn ibn Salih informed us, from Abu ʿAqil, from Jabir, who said: "The straight path is Islam, and it is wider than what lies between the heaven and the earth." The straight path is Islam only because every religion and way other than Islam is not straight.

ʿAsim al-Ahwal narrated from Abu al-ʿAliya al-Riyahi: it is the way of the Prophet (ﷺ) and his two companions.

ʿAsim said: I mentioned that to al-Hasan, and he said: "Abu al-ʿAliya spoke truthfully and gave good counsel."

Bakr ibn Abdullah al-Muzani said: I saw the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) in a dream, and I asked him about al-Sirat al-Mustaqim, and he said: "My sunnah and the sunnah of the Rightly Guided Caliphs after me."

Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: it means the path of the truth.

Al-Suddi said: "He guided us to a religion by which its follower enters Paradise, is never punished in the Fire, and whose emergence from his grave is into Paradise."

Muhammad ibn al-Hanafiyya said: it is the religion of Allah which He accepts from none of His servants other than it.

Abu Muhammad Abdullah ibn Muhammad ibn Abdullah al-Ayni informed us, Abu al-Husayn Muhammad ibn ʿUthman al-Nusaybi informed us in Baghdad, Abu al-Qasim [...] [blank in the photographed manuscript; what is given here is the likely reading] ibn Nahhar informed us, Abu Hafs al-Mustamli informed us, my father informed us, Hamid ibn Sahl informed us, Abdullah ibn Muhammad al-Ajali informed us, Ibrahim ibn Jabir informed us, from Muslim ibn Hayyan, from Abu Burayda, regarding the saying of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿Guide us to the straight path﴾, he said: "The path of Muhammad (ﷺ) and his family (peace be upon them)."

ʿAbd al-ʿAziz ibn Yahya said: it means the path of the great majority (al-sawad al-aʿzam). Abu Bakr al-Warraq said: it means a path along which desires do not deviate to the right or left. Muhammad ibn ʿAli al-Nahdi said: it means the path of fear and hope. Abu ʿUthman al-Darani said: it means the path of servitude.

I heard Abu al-Qasim al-Hasan ibn Muhammad say: I heard Abu Nasr Mansur ibn Abdullah Bahrat say: I heard Abu al-Hasan Umar ibn Wasil al-ʿAnbari say: I heard Sahl ibn Abdullah al-Tustari say: it is the path of the Sunnah and the Community, because innovation cannot be straight.

Abu al-Qasim al-Hasan ibn Muhammad ibn al-Hasan al-Mufassir informed us: Abu al-ʿAbbas Muhammad ibn Yaʿqub al-Asamm informed us: Ahmad ibn Abd al-Jabbar al-ʿAtaridi informed us: Abu Bakr ibn ʿAyyash informed us, from ʿAsim, from Zirr, from Abu Wa'il, from Abdullah, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) drew two lines, one line to his right and one line to his left, then said: "These are the paths, and on each of them is a devil calling to it; and this is the path of Allah." Then he recited: ﴿And that this is My path, straight, so follow it, and do not follow other ways, lest they separate you from His way﴾ [Surah al-An'am 6:153].

Abdullah ibn Hamid informed us, Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Yusuf informed us, Mu'ammar ibn Sufyan al-Saghir informed us, Ya'qub ibn Sufyan al-Kabir informed us, Abu Salih Abdullah ibn Salih informed us, Mu'awiya ibn Salih informed us that Abd al-Rahman ibn Jubayr ibn Nasr narrated to him from his father Jubayr, from Nawwas ibn Mu'adh, from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), that he said: "Allah struck an example of a straight path (ṣiraṭan mustaqiman). On both sides of the path are lowered curtains, and in them are open doors, and over the doors are lowered curtains. At the entrance of the path is a caller saying: 'O people, enter the path and do not deviate.' And a caller calls from above the path; when someone wants to open any of those doors, he says: 'Woe to you, do not open it, for if you open it you will enter it.' The path is Islam. The curtains are the limits of Allah, the open doors are the prohibitions of Allah, the caller at the entrance of the path is the Book of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, and the caller from above is the admonition of Allah in the heart of every believer."

Commentary of al-Tha'alibi (al-Jawahir al-Hisan) on surah 1, verse 7 (part 1 of 3):

"The path" (ṣirāṭ) is a substitute (badal) for the first (ṣirāṭ in the previous verse). "Those upon whom You have bestowed favour" means: the path of those upon whom You have bestowed favour with success, protection, monotheism and guidance, and they are the prophets and the believers whom God Most High mentioned in His saying:

﴿And whoever obeys God and the Messenger, those are with the ones upon whom God has bestowed favour, of the prophets, the truthful, the martyrs and the righteous; and excellent companions are they.﴾

Ibn 'Abbas said: They are the people of Moses and Jesus, before they changed the blessings of God upon them.

Shahr ibn Hawshab said: They are the Companions of the Messenger (ﷺ), may God be pleased with them, and his household (peace be upon them). 'Ikrima said: "upon whom You have bestowed favour" means by steadfastness in faith and uprightness.

'Ali ibn al-Husayn ibn Dawud said: "upon whom You have bestowed favour" means by thankfulness in times of ease and patience in times of hardship. And he said: ... [[blank in the manuscript.]] ... ibn ... [[blank in the manuscript.]] ...: by what Muhammad (ﷺ) has established. Al-Husayn ibn al-Fadl said: it means You completed the blessing upon them, for how many a one has been blessed ... [[blank in the manuscript.]] ...

The root of ni'ma (blessing) is abundance and increase. It is said: "I pounded the medicine, so I made its pounding abundant (anʿamtu daqqahu)", meaning I went to the extreme in pounding it. From this is the saying of the Arabs, the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "The people of Paradise look upon the chamber within it as one looks upon the bright star in the eastern or western horizon of the sky, and indeed Abu Bakr and 'Umar are among them, and they have been blessed (wa-an'amā)." [[al-Jami' al-Saghir: 2/203.]] [32]

That is, they increased upon it. Abu 'Amr said: they went to the extreme in good.

Al-Sadiq recited: "the path of those whom You have blessed" (ṣirāṭa man anʿamta ʿalayhim), and 'Amr ibn al-Zubayr and 'Ali also recited thus. The letter lam (ʿalayhim) governs what follows it.

For ʿalayhim there are seven readings:

The first: ʿalayhim, with a kasra on the ha' and a sukun on the mim, which is the reading of the common people.

The second: ʿalayhum, with a damma on the ha' and a sukun on the mim, which is the reading of al-A'mash and Hamza. It is narrated from the Prophet (ﷺ) and 'Umar (may God be pleased with him).

The third: ʿalayhumu, with a damma on the ha' and the mim, with the addition of a waw, which is the reading of 'Isa ibn 'Umar and Ibn Abi Ishaq.

The fourth: ʿalayhimo, with a kasra on the ha' and a damma on the mim, with the addition of a waw, which is the reading of Ibn Kathir and al-A'raj.

The fifth: ʿalayhimi, with a kasra on the ha' and the mim, with the addition of a ya', which is the reading of al-Hasan.

The sixth: ʿalayhimu, with a kasra on the ha' and a damma on the mim, the damma being brief (mukhtalasa), which is the narration of ʿAbd Allah ibn ʿAta' al-Khaffaf from Abu 'Amr.

The seventh: ʿalayhimi, with a kasra on the ha' and the mim, which is the reading of 'Amr ibn Hamid.

Whoever puts a damma on the ha' returns it to the original, since if it stood alone it would be pronounced with a damma at the beginning of speech. Whoever puts a kasra on it does so because of the following quiescent ya'. Whoever puts a kasra on the ha' and a sukun on the mim finds the damma heavy alongside the adjacent quiescent ya', and the ya' is a sister of the kasra, and moving from damma to kasra is heavy. Whoever puts a damma on both the ha' and the mim follows the damma.

Whoever puts a kasra on the ha' and a damma on the mim: he puts a kasra on the ha' because of the ya', and keeps the damma on the mim as in the original; the brief pronunciation is for lightness, and the addition of the waw and ya' is for harmony (al-ittibā'). And God knows best. A poet said concerning the brief mim:

"By God, were it not for a branch of nobility
Of a standing position among the clan, of maternal and paternal uncles,
You would have been among them a man without foot."
[[Kitab al-Munammaq of al-Baghdadi: 130.]]

"Not of those who have earned anger" (ghayr al-maghḍūb): ghayr is an attribute of "those" (alladhīna). The definite is not described by the indefinite, nor the indefinite by the definite, except that alladhīna is not a specific definite, but it is in the position of your saying: "I pass by a truthful person, not a liar," as if you said: one who speaks truth, not one who lies. It is not permissible to say: "I passed by ʿAbd Allah, not the witty."

The meaning of his statement: other than the path of those upon whom You have been angry.

On the meaning of anger: They differed concerning the meaning of God's anger, the Mighty and Majestic. Some people said: it is the intention to take vengeance upon the disobedient. It was said: it is a kind of punishment opposed to contentment. It was said: it is blaming the disobedient for the ugliness of their deeds.

The anger of God Most High does not reach the disobedient among the believers, but reaches the disbelievers.

"Nor of those who are astray" from guidance.

The root of ḍalāl is perdition. It is said: "The water was lost (ḍalla) in the milk" when it became hidden and disappeared; and "a man is ḍāll" when he misses the road; and "mudallal" when he does not turn toward good. The poet said:

"Did you not ask, and would the abodes inform you
About the tribe that went astray (al-mudallal), where they travelled?"
[[Tafsir al-Qurtubi: 1/150.]]

Al-Zajjaj and others said: It is permissible to conjoin with "lā" after ghayr because ghayr includes the sense of negation, so it means "lā": its import is "ghayr al-maghḍūb ʿalayhim wa-ghayr al-ḍāllīn," just as you say: "so-and-so is not good (muḥsin) nor graceful (mujmil)." But when ghayr means "siwā" (other than), it is not permissible to conjoin with "lā" after it, because in my view it is not permissible in speech to say "siwā ʿAbd Allāh wa-lā Zayd." Al-Khalil ibn Ahmad narrated from Ibn Kathir: ghayra al-maghḍūbi (in the accusative).

ʿUmar ibn al-Khattab and ʿAli ibn Abi Talib, may God be pleased with them both, recited: "wa-ghayr al-ḍāllīn." Al-Sakhtiyani recited "wa-la al-ḍāllīn" with a hamza due to the meeting of two quiescent letters. And God knows best.

As for the tafsir:

ʿAbd Allah ibn Hamid informed us: Ahmad ibn ʿAbd Allah al-Muzani informed us: Muhammad ibn ʿAbd Allah ibn Sulayman informed us: Ahmad ibn Hanbal and Muhammad ibn Dinar informed us, both saying: Muhammad ibn Ja'far narrated to us from Shu'ba from Simak, who said: I heard ʿAbbad ibn Habish from ʿAdi ibn Hatim from the Prophet (ﷺ): "ghayri al-maghḍūbi ʿalayhim" – he said: "the Jews," and "wa-lā al-ḍāllīn" – he said: "the Christians." [[Tafsir Ibn Kathir: 1/32.]] [33]

Abu al-Qasim al-Habibi informed us: Abu Zakariyya al-ʿAnbari informed us: Muhammad ibn ʿAbd Allah al-Warraq narrated to us: Ishaq ibn Ibrahim informed us: ʿAbd al-Razzaq informed us from Ma'mar ibn ʿAbd Allah ibn Badil al-ʿAqili from ʿAbd Allah ibn Shaqiq, that he informed him from one who heard the Messenger of God (ﷺ), while he was at Wadi al-Qura on his horse, when a man from the Qayn asked him: "O Messenger of God, who are these who fight you?" He said: "Those upon whom anger is incurred." And he pointed to the Jews. He said: "And who is the other group?" He said: "The astray," and he pointed to the Christians. [[Tafsir Ibn Kathir: 1/32, with slight variation.]] [34]

Confirming this hadith is God's judgement of anger upon the Jews in His saying: ﴿Shall I inform you of something worse than that as a recompense from God? Those whom God has cursed and upon whom He has been angry﴾ [[Surat al-Ma'ida: 60.]], and His judgement of straying upon the Christians in His saying: ﴿And do not follow the desires of a people who had already gone astray﴾ [[Surat al-Ma'ida: 77.]].

Al-Waqidi said: "those upon whom anger is incurred" through opposition and disobedience, and "nor those who are astray" from religion and faith.

Al-Tustari said: "those upon whom anger is incurred" – innovation, and "nor those who are astray" – from the Sunna.

Section on Amin

The recommended practice is that the reciter says, after finishing the recitation of the Opening (Fatiha), "Amin," whether in prayer or outside prayer, because of what

ʿAbd Allah ibn Hamid al-Isfahani informed us: Muhammad ibn Ja'far al-Mutayri informed us: al-Hasan ibn ʿAli ibn ʿAffan al-ʿAmiri narrated to us: Abu Dawud narrated to us from Sufyan; and ʿAbd Allah informed us, he said: and ʿAbdus ibn al-Husayn informed us: Abu Hatim al-Razi narrated to us: Ibn Kathir narrated to us: Sufyan informed us from Salama from Hujr Abu al-ʿAnbas al-Hadrami from Abu Qa'il ibn Hujr, who said: When the Messenger of God (ﷺ) recited "wa-lā al-ḍāllīn," he said: "Amin," and raised his voice with it. [[Musnad Ahmad: 4/316.]] [35]

It is also narrated from him (ﷺ) that he said: "Jibril taught me 'Amin' at the end of my reading of the Opening of the Book." [36]

And he said: "It is like a seal upon the book." [[Tafsir al-Qurtubi: 1/127-128.]]

It has two forms: "amīn" with a short alif, and a poet recited:

"He withdrew from me when I asked him
'Amin,' so God increased what is between us in distance."

And "āmīn" with a long alif, and a poet recited:

"O Lord, do not deprive me of her love forever,
and may God have mercy on a servant who says: amin."
[[Zad al-Masir: 1/12; Tafsir al-Qurtubi: 1/128.]]

It is built on fatḥa, like "ayna."

They differed concerning its interpretation.

Abu al-Qasim al-Hasan ibn Muhammad ibn Ja'far informed us: Abu al-ʿAbbas Muhammad ibn Ishaq ibn Ayyub informed us: al-Hasan ibn ʿAli ibn Ziyad narrated to us: ʿUbayd ibn Yaʿish narrated to us from Muhammad ibn al-Fadl from al-Kalbi from Abu Salih from Ibn ʿAbbas, who said: I asked the Messenger of God (ﷺ) about the meaning of "amin." He said: "O Lord, do it." [37] [[al-Durr al-Manthur: 1/17; Fath al-Qadir: 1/26.]]

Ibn ʿAbbas and Qatada said: its meaning is: "Thus let it be."

ʿAbd Allah ibn Hamid al-Wazzan informed us: Makki ibn ʿAbdan informed us: ʿAbd Allah ibn Hatim narrated to us: ʿAbd Allah ibn Numayr narrated to us: Sufyan informed us from Mansur from Hilal ibn Yasaf, who said: "Amin" is one of the names of God Most High, and [with this] [[In the manuscript: dhalika.]] Mujahid said.

Sahl ibn ʿAbd Allah said: its meaning: no one is capable of this besides You. Muhammad ibn ʿAli al-Nahdi said: its meaning: do not disappoint our hope.

ʿAtiyya al-ʿAwfi said: "Amin" is a word that is not Arabic; it is Hebrew or Syriac, then the Arabs spoke it and it became a language of theirs. ʿAbd al-Rahman ibn Zayd said: "Amin" is a treasure from the treasures of the Throne; none knows its interpretation except God, the Mighty and Majestic.

Abu Bakr al-Warraq said: "Amin" is a strength for supplication and a drawing down of mercy.

al-Dahhak ibn Muzahim said: "Amin" is four letters detached from the names of God Most High, and it is the seal of the Lord of the Worlds, with which the acquittals of the people of Paradise and the acquittals of the people of the Fire are sealed, and it is the passport by which they pass into Paradise and the Fire. [[Fayd al-Qadir: 1/80, no. 20.]]

What indicates this is what

Abu al-Qasim al-Hasan ibn Muhammad ibn Ja'far informed us: Abu al-Hasan Muhammad ibn Mahmud ibn ʿAbd Allah narrated to us: Muhammad ibn ʿAli al-Hafiz narrated to us: ʿAbd Allah ibn Ahmad ibn Hamawayh narrated to us: Sa'id ibn Jubayr narrated to us: al-Mu'ammal ibn ʿAbd al-Rahman ibn ʿAyyash al-Thaqafi narrated to us, from Abu Umayya ibn Ya'la al-Thaqafi, from Sa'id al-Maqbari, from Abu Hurayra, that the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "Amin is the seal of the Lord of the Worlds upon His believing servants." [38] [[Kitab al-Du'a of al-Tabarani: 89; Kanz al-'Ummal: 1/559, no. 2512.]]

Muhammad ibn ʿAbd Allah ibn Hamdun ibn al-Fadl informed us, with my reading to him in Safar of the year four hundred and eight: Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn al-Husayn ibn al-Sharqi informed us: Muhammad ibn Yahya, ʿAbd al-Rahman ibn Bishr and Ahmad ibn Yusuf narrated to us, they said: ʿAbd al-Razzaq narrated to us, Ma'mar informed us from Hammam ibn Munabbih, who said: Abu Hurayra narrated to us from the Messenger of God (ﷺ), who said: "When one of you says amin and the angels in the heaven say it, and their saying coincides, he is forgiven what preceded of his sins." [39] [[Musnad Ahmad: 2/312.]]

Abu al-Qasim al-Hasan ibn Muhammad ibn Ja'far narrated to us: Muhammad Abu al-Hasan Muhammad ibn al-Hasan of Harat informed us: Raja' ibn ʿAbd Allah narrated to us: Malik ibn Sulaym narrated to us, from Sa'id ibn Salim, from Ibn Jurayj, from ʿAta', who said: "Amin" is a supplication. [And from him, from] the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: "The Jews have not envied you for anything as they have envied you for amin and for your greeting one another." [40] [[al-Musannaf of ʿAbd al-Razzaq: 2/98, no. 2649.]]

Wahb ibn Munabbih said: "Amin" has four letters; God creates from each letter an angel who says: "O God, forgive whoever says amin."

Section on the names of this surah

It has ten names, and the multiplicity of names indicates the nobility of the named:

The first: al-Fatiha al-Kitab (The Opening of the Book). It is so called because it opens the mushafs, teaching, and recitation in prayer, and it opens with the verse that things begin with, for blessing and benediction, which is the basmala. It was said: it was so named because praise is the opening of every book, just as it is the opening of the Qur'an. Al-Husayn ibn al-Fadl said: because it is the first surah sent down from heaven.

The second: Surat al-Hamd (the Surah of Praise), because it mentions praise, as surahs are named al-A'raf, al-Anfal, al-Tawba and similar.

The third: Umm al-Kitab and al-Qur'an (the Mother of the Book and the Qur'an). It is so called because it is the beginning of the Qur'an and of the revealed books, and all the sciences it contains are gathered in this surah, so it is the origin of them, as a mother is to a child. It was said: it was so named because it is the best of the surahs of the Qur'an, just as Mecca is called Umm al-Qura because it is the noblest of cities. It was said: it was so named because it precedes the surahs of the Qur'an, so it is the origin and leader of the surahs that follow it, just as Umm al-Qura is the origin of all cities, from beneath which the earth was spread. It was said: it was so named because it is the gathering of sciences and goods, just as the brain is called the mother of the head because it is the gathering of the senses and benefits.

I heard Abu al-Qasim al-Hasan ibn Muhammad al-Mufassir say: I heard Abu Bakr al-Qaffal say: I heard Abu Bakr al-Baridi say: "al-umm" in the speech of the Arabs is the banner which the army sets up.

Qays ibn al-Khatim said:
"We set up our umm until they scattered,
and after their familiarity they became a flock."

So the Qur'an's Umm was named because the refuge of the people of faith is to it, as the army's refuge is to the banner. The Arabs call the earth umm, because the return of creation is to it in their lives and after their deaths. Umayya ibn Abi al-Salt said:
"The earth is our refuge, and it was our mother;
in it are our graves, and in it we are born."
[[Tafsir al-Qurtubi: 1/112.]]

Abu al-Qasim recited to me: Abu al-Husayn al-Muzaffar Muhammad ibn Ghalib al-Hamdani recited to us, he said: Abu Bakr ibn al-Anbari recited to us, he said: my father recited to us, he said: Ahmad ibn ʿUbayda recited to me:
"We take refuge in a mother who is bound with a band,
as for her she has a noble nose and a tail,
and a barrier which the wrath does not conceal
from the clouds, she clothes herself and veils."
[[Lisan al-Arab: 15/168, abridged.]]

He means: he set it up as it was described for her. The Fatiha was called umm for these meanings. Al-Husayn ibn al-Fadl said: it was so named because it is the leader of the whole Qur'an, recited in every [prayer], and it precedes every surah, just as Umm al-Qura is the leader of the people of Islam. Ibn Kaysan said: it was so named because it is complete in excellence.

The fourth: al-Sab' al-Mathani (the seven oft-repeated), and its explanation will come in its place, God willing.

The fifth: al-Wafiya (the Complete),

Abu al-Qasim al-Hasan ibn Muhammad al-Nisaburi narrated to us: my father narrated to us from his mother, from Muhammad ibn Nafi' al-Sanjari, Abu Yazid Mahbub al-Shami narrated to us: ʿAbd al-Jabbar ibn al-ʿAla' narrated to us, who said:
Sufyan ibn ʿUyayna used to call the Opening of the Book "al-Wafiya," and its explanation is that it is not halved and does not tolerate being partially recited, except that every surah of the Qur'an, if half of it is recited in one rak'a and the other half in another rak'a, it is permissible; but if the Fatiha is halved and recited in two rak'as, it is not permissible.

The sixth: al-Kafiya (the Sufficient),

Abu al-Qasim al-Sadusi informed us: Abu Ja'far Muhammad ibn Malik al-Masuri informed us: Abu ʿAbd Allah Muhammad ibn ʿImran narrated to us, he said: Suhayl ibn [Muhammad] [[So it appears.]] narrated to us, ʿAfif ibn Salim narrated to us, who said: I asked ʿAbd Allah ibn Yahya ibn Abi Kathir about reciting the Fatiha behind the imam, and he said: Are you asking about the Sufficient (al-Kafiya)?

I said: And what is the Sufficient? He said: Do you not know that it suffices in place of others, and others do not suffice in its place. Beware of praying except with it.

What confirms this report is what

al-Hasan ibn Muhammad ibn Ja'far al-Mufassir narrated to us: ʿAbd al-Rahman ibn ʿUmar ibn Malik al-Jawhari in Marw narrated to us: my father narrated to us: Ahmad ibn Yasar narrated to us, from Muhammad ibn ʿAbbad al-Iskandarani, from Ashhab ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAziz, from Ibn ʿUyayna, from al-Zuhri, from Mahmud ibn al-Rabi', from ʿUbada ibn al-Samit, who said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "Umm al-Qur'an is a substitute for other than it, and other than it is not a substitute for it." [[Kanz al-'Ummal: 1/558; Irwa' al-Ghalil: 2/11.]] [41]

The seventh: al-Asas (the Foundation),

Abu al-Qasim al-Husayn ibn Muhammad al-Mudhakkir narrated to us: Abu ʿAmr ibn al-Muʿabbir Muhammad ibn al-Fadl al-Qadi in Marw narrated to us: Abu Hurayra Muzahim ibn Muhammad ibn Shারida al-Kashshi narrated to us: Jarud ibn Mu'adh narrated to us: Waki' informed us, who said: A man came to al-Sha'bi and complained to him of a pain in the flank, and he said:

Tafsir text continued:

Hold fast to the foundation of the Qur'an." He said: "And what is the foundation of the Qur'an?" He said: "The Opening of the Book (al-Fatiha)." Al-Sha'bi said: "I heard ʿAbd Allah ibn ʿAbbas say on more than one occasion: 'Every thing has a foundation. The foundation of prosperity is Mecca, for the earth was spread out from it. The foundation of the heavens is Gharibā',[[In Tafsir al-Qurtubi (1/113): ʿAryba.]] which is the seventh heaven. The foundation of the earth is ʿAjība, which is the lowest seventh earth. The foundation of the Gardens is the Garden of Eden, which is the navel of the Gardens, and the Gardens were founded upon it. The foundation of the Fire is Jahannam, which is the lowest seventh level, and the levels were founded upon it. The foundation of creation is Adam (peace be upon him). The foundation of the prophets is Noah (peace be upon him). The foundation of the Children of Israel is Jacob. The foundation of the scriptures is the Qur'an. The foundation of the Qur'an is al-Fatiha, and the foundation of al-Fatiha is ﴿In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful﴾. So if you fall ill or suffer a complaint, then recite al-Fatiha and you will be healed.'"

The eighth: healing.

Abu al-Qasim ibn Abi Bakr al-Mukattib related to us, in wording, saying: Abu ʿAli Hamid ibn Muhammad ibn ʿAbd Allah al-Raffa' related to us, saying: Muhammad ibn Ayyub al-Waqidi informed us, saying: Abu ʿAmr ibn al-ʿAla' related to us, saying: Salam al-Tawil related to us, from Zayd al-ʿAmmi, from Muhammad ibn Sirin, from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, who said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "The Opening of the Book is a healing from every poison."[[Tafsir al-Qurtubi: 1/112.]] [42]

And Muhammad ibn al-Qasim al-Faqih informed us, saying: Abu al-Husayn Muhammad ibn al-Hasan al-Saffar al-Faqih related to us, saying: Abu al-ʿAbbas al-Sarraj related to us, saying: Qutayba ibn Sa'id related to us, saying: Muʿawiya ibn Salih related to us, from Abu Sulayman, who said:

Some of the Companions of the Messenger of God (ﷺ) passed, during one of their expeditions, by a man who was paralysed and sitting cross-legged. Some of them recited a portion of the Qur'an into his ear, and he was cured. The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "It is the Mother of the Qur'an, and it is a healing from every disease."[[Sunan al-Darimi: 2/445, with variation.]] [43]

Ahmad ibn Abi al-Khawjani informed us, saying: al-Haytham ibn Kulayb al-Shami informed us, saying: ʿIsa ibn Ahmad al-ʿAsqalani related to us, saying: al-Nadr ibn Shumayl informed us, saying: Sa'id ibn al-Hajjaj informed us, from ʿAbd Allah ibn Abi al-Safar, from al-Sha'bi, from Kharija ibn al-Salt al-Tamimi, from his paternal uncle, who said: My uncle came from the presence of the Messenger of God (ﷺ), and they passed by a tribe of Bedouins, who said: "We see that you have come from this Messenger. There is among us a man who is mad and possessed. Do you have any medicine or incantation (ruqya)?" My uncle said: "Yes." So the man was brought, and my uncle began to recite the Mother of the Qur'an and spit upon him; whenever he finished it, he spat. He continued this for three days, and it was as if he had been released from the mountains. My uncle said: "They gave me a reward for it, and I said: 'We will not take it until we ask the Messenger of God (ﷺ).'" So he asked him, and he said: "Take it, for by the permissible you have used an incantation. You have indeed taken a reward for a true incantation."[[With variation in Sunan Abi Dawud: 2/129, no. 3421.]]

The ninth: prayer. Reports have been transmitted in succession that God Most High named this surah, and it is known that there is no prayer except with it.

ʿAbd Allah ibn Hamid and Ahmad ibn Yusuf informed us, by my reading to them, saying: Makki ibn ʿAbd Allah informed us, saying: Muhammad ibn Yahya related to us, saying: "And in what I read to Ibn Nafiʿ, and Mutarrif related to us from Malik ibn Anas, from al-ʿAlaʾ ibn ʿAbd al-Rahman, that he heard Abu al-Sa'ib, the freedman of Hisham ibn Zahra, say: I heard Abu Hurayra say:

I heard the Messenger of God (ﷺ) say: "God, Mighty and Majestic, says: 'I have divided the prayer'—meaning this surah—'between Me and My servant into two halves. Half is for Me, and half is for My servant. When the servant recites "All praise is for God, Lord of the Worlds," God says: "My servant has praised Me." When he says "The Most Gracious, the Most Merciful," God says: "My servant has extolled Me." When he says "Master of the Day of Judgment," God says: "My servant has glorified Me." When the servant says "You alone we worship, and You alone we ask for help," God says: "This verse is between Me and My servant, and for My servant is what he asks." When the servant says "Guide us to the straight path," to the end, God says: "This is for My servant, and for My servant is what he asks.'"[[Tafsir al-Qurtubi: 1/121; Musnad Ahmad: 2/285, with variation.]] [44]

The tenth: it is a surah that teaches how to ask, because God Most High taught His servants in it the etiquette of supplication, beginning with praise and then supplication, and this is the means of success and prosperity.

On the obligation of reciting this surah in the prayer.

ʿAbd Allah ibn Hamid informed us, saying: Muhammad ibn Jaʿfar al-Tabari informed us, saying: Bishr ibn Mutayr related to us, saying: Sufyan related to us, saying: al-ʿAlaʾ ibn ʿAbd al-Rahman related to us, from his father, that he heard Abu Hurayra narrate from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "Whoever prays a prayer and does not recite in it the Opening of the Book"—in the source: "the Mother of the Qur'an"—"then it is deficient (khidaj)," three times, "incomplete."[[Sharh Muslim: 4/101; Tafsir al-Qurtubi: 1/119.]] [45]

ʿAbd Allah informed us, saying: Ibn ʿAbbas informed us, saying: ʿAbd al-Rahman ibn Bishr related to us, saying: Ibn ʿUyayna related to us, from al-Zuhri, from Mahmud ibn al-Rabiʿ, from ʿUbada ibn al-Samit, who said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "There is no prayer for one who does not recite in it the Opening of the Book."[46]

ʿAbd Allah informed us, ʿAbdus ibn al-Husayn informed us, saying: Abu Hatim al-Razi related to us, saying: Abu Qabisa related to us, saying: Sufyan related to us, from Jaʿfar ibn ʿAli, the seller of mattresses, from Abu Hurayra, who said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) commanded me to proclaim: "There is no prayer except with the recitation of the Opening of the Book."[[Musnad Ahmad: 2/428.]] [47]

ʿAbd Allah informed us, Abu Bakr Ahmad ibn Ishaq informed us, Abu al-Muthanna informed us, saying: Musaddad related to us, saying: ʿAbd al-Warith ibn Handhala al-Sadusi related to us, who said: I said to ʿIkrima: "I sometimes recite in the Maghrib prayer 'Say: I seek refuge in the Lord of the Daybreak' and 'Say: I seek refuge in the Lord of Mankind,' and people criticise me for that." He said: "Glory be to God! Recite them, for they are from the Qur'an." Then he said: "Ibn ʿAbbas related to us that the Prophet (ﷺ) went out and prayed two rak'as, reciting in them nothing but the Opening of the Book, and he added nothing to it."

Abu al-Qasim al-Habibi informed us, saying: Abu al-ʿAbbas al-Asamm related to us, saying: al-Rabiʿ ibn Sulayman informed us, saying: al-Shafiʿi related to us, saying: Sufyan related to us, from al-Zuhri, from Mahmud ibn al-Rabiʿ, from ʿUbada ibn al-Samit, that the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "There is no prayer for one who does not recite the Opening of the Book."[[Musnad Ahmad: 5/314; Kitab al-Musnad li-l-Shafiʿi: 36.]]

Those who permitted prayer without it argued with His saying: ﴿So recite what is easy of the Qur'an﴾.

ʿAbd Allah ibn Hamid, by my reading to him, informed us: Abu Bakr Ahmad ibn Ishaq al-Faqih informed us: Abu al-Muthanna informed us: Musaddad related to us: Yahya ibn Sa'id related to us, from ʿAbd Allah ibn ʿUmar, who said: Sa'id ibn Abi Sa'id related to us, from his father, from Abu Hurayra, that the Messenger of God (ﷺ) entered the mosque. A man entered, prayed, then came and greeted the Messenger of God (ﷺ), who said: "Go back and pray, for you have not prayed." This was done three times. The man said: "By the One who sent you with truth as a prophet, I do not know better than this, so teach me." He said: "When you stand up for prayer, say the takbir, then recite what is easy for you of the Qur'an, then bow."[48][[Musnad Ahmad: 2/437.]]

This wording may mean that every thing to which the name "Qur'an" applies is intended, but in ignorance it is a particular surah that is meant. Since it admits of two meanings, we looked and found that the Prophet (ﷺ) prayed with the Opening of the Book and commanded it, and [he was severe] [[Omitted in the manuscript; what we have written appears to be correct.]] toward whoever abandoned it. So this report is mujmal (general or unspecified), while the reports we have cited are mufassar (explicit), and the general points to the explicit. This is like His saying: ﴿So whoever enjoys the ʿUmra until the Hajj, let him give what is easy of the offering﴾,[[Surah al-Baqara: 196.]] and then no one permitted [leaving out the offering] [[So the text appears to read.]], rather the Messenger of God (ﷺ) established it by the description that it must not be one-eyed, lame, or defective. Likewise, by His saying, Mighty and Majestic, and the saying of the Messenger of God (ﷺ), what was explained by the description he specified is that the Surah of Praise is to be recited as well as one can, and as much as one can if one cannot do it well. Based on the reason for which they required reciting a complete verse together with His saying "what is easy," there is a sound basis, as the apparent meaning indicates knowledge. And God knows best.

Mention of the obligation of reciting it upon the follower (al-ma'mum), just as it is obligatory upon the imam, and the disagreement of the jurists about it:

Malik ibn Anas said: It is obligatory for him to recite it if the imam recites quietly, but if the imam recites aloud, then nothing is required of him.

Al-Shafiʿi said the same in his earlier view (al-qadim), but in his later view (al-jadid) he said: it is required of him to recite, whether the imam recites quietly or aloud. Abu Hanifa and his companions said: he is not required to recite, whether the imam recites quietly or aloud.

The Muslims agreed that his prayer is valid if he recites behind the imam.[[See al-Sharh al-Kabir of Ibn Qudama: 2/12.]]

The evidence that reciting is obligatory upon the follower just as it is upon the imam is what:

ʿAbd Allah ibn Hamid informed us, saying: Makki ibn ʿAbd Allah informed us, saying: Abu al-Azhar related to us, saying: Yaʿqub ibn Ibrahim ibn Saʿd related to us, saying: my father related to us, from Abu Ishaq, saying: Makhul related to us. And ʿAbd Allah informed us, saying: Ahmad ibn ʿAbd al-Rahman ibn Sahl informed us, saying: Sahl ibn ʿAmmar related to us, saying: Yazid ibn Harun related to us, saying: Muhammad ibn Ishaq informed us, from Makhul, from Mahmud ibn al-Rabiʿ, from ʿUbada ibn al-Samit, who said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) led us in the dawn prayer, and the recitation was difficult for him. When the Messenger of God (ﷺ) finished his prayer, he turned his face toward us and said: "I see that you recite behind me?" [In the source: "behind your imam."] We said: "Yes, by God, O Messenger of God, we do." He said: "Do not do so, except with the Mother of the Book, for there is no prayer for one who does not recite it."[[Sahih Ibn Khuzayma: 3/36.]] [49]

This is the view of ʿUmar, ʿUthman, ʿAli, Ibn ʿAbbas, Jabir, Ibn Masʿud, ʿImran ibn Husayn, Zayd ibn Thabit, Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, ʿUbada ibn al-Samit, Hisham ibn ʿAmir, Muʿadh ibn Jabal, Ubayy ibn Kaʿb, ʿAbd Allah ibn ʿUmar, Abu al-Darda', ʿAʾisha, Abu Hurayra, and a great company of the Successors and the leading Muslim scholars. It is reported from all of them that they regarded reciting behind the imam as obligatory.

The basis of the earlier view is what Sufyan related from ʿAsim ibn Abi al-Najud, from Dhakwan, from Abu Hurayra and ʿAʾisha, that they used to command reciting behind the imam when he does not recite aloud.

Abu Hanifa and his companions argued with what:

ʿAbd Allah ibn Hamid informed us, saying: Abu Bakr Ahmad ibn Ishaq al-Faqih informed us, saying: Muhammad ibn ʿUthman ibn Abi Shayba informed us, saying: al-Walid ibn Hammad al-Lu'lu'i related to us: al-Hasan ibn Ziyad al-Lu'lu'i related to us: Abu Hanifa related to us, from al-Hasan, from ʿAbd Allah ibn Shaddad ibn al-Hadi, from Jabir ibn ʿAbd Allah, who said: The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Whoever prays behind an imam, the recitation of the imam is his recitation."[50][[Nasb al-Raya: 2/16.]]

And ʿAbd Allah ibn Hamid informed us, saying: Abu Bakr ibn Ishaq informed us, saying: Muhammad ibn Ayyub informed us, saying: Ahmad ibn Yunus informed us, saying: al-Hasan ibn Salih related to us, from Jabir al-Ju'fi, from Abu al-Zubayr, from Jabir, from the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: "Whoever has an imam, his recitation is the imam's recitation."[51][[Musnad Ahmad: 3/339.]]

As for the report of ʿAbd Allah ibn Shaddad, it is mursal (its chain omits a companion), transmitted as mursal by Shuʿba, Za'ida, Ibn ʿUyayna, Abu ʿAwana, Israʾil, Qays, Jarir and Abu al-Ahwas, and a mursal report does not establish proof. Al-Walid ibn Hammad and al-Hasan are not known. As for the report of Jabir al-Ju'fi, it is discarded. Zaʾida said: "Jabir is a liar." Abu Hanifa said: "I have never seen anyone more lying than Jabir." Ibn ʿUyayna said: "Jabir did not have certainty about the return (to life)."

Shuʿba said: "Jabir said to me: 'I entered upon Muhammad ibn ʿAli, and he gave me a drink, and I memorised twenty thousand hadiths.'"

There is no disagreement among the transmitters that his narration cannot be used as proof.

And it has been reported from Jabir ibn ʿAbd Allah something contrary to these reports:

ʿAbd Allah ibn Hamid informed us, saying: Abu Bakr ibn Ishaq informed us, saying: ʿAbd Allah ibn Muhammad related to us, saying: Muhammad ibn Yahya related to us, saying: Saʿd ibn ʿAmir informed us, from Shuʿba, from Mis'ar, from Yazid ibn al-Faqir, from Jabir ibn ʿAbd Allah, who said: "We used to recite in the noon and afternoon prayers behind the imam." It is inconceivable that Jabir ibn ʿAbd Allah would narrate from the Prophet (ﷺ) that the imam's recitation is the follower's recitation, and then recite behind the imam and command it, contrary to the Prophet (ﷺ).

They also argued with what was reported from ʿAsim ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAziz, from Abu Suhayl, from ʿAwwan, from Ibn ʿAbbas, from the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: "The recitation of the imam suffices you, whether he recites aloud or not."[52][[Nasb al-Raya: 2/18; Sunan al-Daraqutni: 1/327, with variation.]]

This hadith too is not affirmed by the people of knowledge of hadith, because it is not the wording of the hadith. The authentic report on this matter is from Abu Hurayra: 

Abu ʿAmr al-Furati informed us, saying: al-Haytham ibn Kulayb informed us, saying: al-ʿAbbas ibn Muhammad al-Duri related to us, saying: Bishr ibn Kalb related to us, saying: Shuʿba related to us, from al-ʿAlaʾ ibn ʿAbd al-Rahman, from his father, from Abu Hurayra, that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Every prayer in which the Opening of the Book is not recited is deficient, deficient, deficient, incomplete."[[Maʿrifa ʿUlum al-Hadith of al-Hakim al-Nisaburi: 132.]] He said: "I said to him: 'What if one is behind the imam?' So he took hold of my forearm and said: 'O Persian—or he said: O son of the Persian—recite it to yourself.'"[53][[Musnad al-Humaydi: 2/430.]]

They also argued with what Abu Ishaq related from Abu al-Ahwas, from ʿAbd Allah, who said: "They used to recite behind the Prophet (ﷺ), and he said: 'You have confused the Qur'an for me.'"[[Majma' al-Zawa'id: 2/110.]]

This report is open to question. Even if it were authentic, the prohibition would be as transmitted by al-Nadr ibn Shumayl:

Yunus ibn Abi Ishaq informed us, from Abu Ishaq, from Abu al-Ahwas, from ʿAbd Allah, that the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said to a people who were reciting the Qur'an and reciting it aloud: "You have confused the Qur'an for me."[54][[Majma' al-Zawa'id: 2/110.]]

So his prohibition of reciting behind the imam aloud contains nothing that prevents reciting quietly. We do not permit reciting aloud behind the imam, because of the bad manners and the evident harm it involves.

Yahya ibn ʿAbd related, from Muhammad ibn Ibrahim, from Abu Hazim, from al-Bayadi, who said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "When one of you stands to pray, he is conversing with his Lord, so let him consider what he converses about, and let none of you raise his voice over another with the Qur'an."[55][[Musnad Ahmad: 2/129; Majma' al-Zawa'id: 2/265, with variation.]]

The evidence for this interpretation is the report of ʿAbd Allah ibn Ziyad al-Ash'ari, who said: "I prayed beside ʿAbd Allah ibn Masʿud behind the imam, and I heard him reciting in the noon and afternoon prayers." Likewise is the answer to their argument from the report of ʿImran ibn Husayn, who said: "The Messenger of God (ﷺ) led us in the noon and afternoon prayers, and when he finished he said: 'Which of you recited "Glorify the name of your Lord, the Most High"?'[[Surah al-A'la: 1.]] A man said: 'I did, and I intended only good.' The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: 'I knew that some of you were disputing it with me.'"[56][[Musnad Ahmad: 4/426.]]

They also argued with the hadith of Abu Hurayra: "When he recites, then listen attentively." Listening attentively (inṣāt) is not merely silence; rather, listening attentively means that you listen well to a thing and then convey it as you heard it. This is indicated by His saying, Most High, in the story of the jinn: ﴿When they came to it, they said: "Be silent (anṣitū)." When it was finished, they returned to their people as warners. They said: "O our people..."﴾[[Surah al-Ahqaf: 29–30.]]

A person may be called one who listens attentively (munṣit) while he is reciting and glorifying, if he does not do so aloud. Do you not see that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Whoever comes to the Friday prayer and listens attentively and does not engage in idle talk until the imam has prayed, will have such-and-such"?[57][[Musnad Ahmad: 4/10; Sunan al-Darimi: 1/363, with variation.]]

So he called him one who listens attentively, even though he was praying and remembering God. It was said to the Prophet (ﷺ): "What do you also say?" He said: "I say: 'O God, wash me of my sins.'"

This shows that listening attentively, which is refraining from reciting aloud (though not necessarily from reciting quietly), is supported by what Abu al-Qasim al-Husayn informed us, saying: Abu al-ʿAbbas al-Asamm related to us, saying: Abu al-Darda' Hashim ibn Muhammad related to us, saying: ʿUbayd ibn al-Sakan related to us, saying: Isma'il ibn ʿAbbas related to us, saying: Muhammad ibn al-Sabbah informed us, from ʿAmr ibn Shu'ayb, from his father, from his grandfather, who said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "Whoever prays an obligatory prayer or a voluntary prayer, let him recite the Mother of the Qur'an."[[Al-Musannaf of ʿAbd al-Razzaq: 2/133; Kanz al-ʿUmmal: 7/442, no. 19688.]]

He said: "I said: 'O Messenger of God, I am sometimes behind the imam.'" He (ﷺ) said: "Recite when he is silent; the imam was only appointed to be followed."[58][[Musnad Ahmad: 2/314; Sunan al-Darimi: 1/287; Sahih al-Bukhari: 1/100.]]

This has been transmitted by reliable and trustworthy narrators from Abu Hurayra, such as al-A'raj, Hammam ibn Munabbih, Qays ibn Abi Hazim, Abu Salih, Sa'id al-Maqburi, al-Qasim ibn Muhammad and Abu Salama, and they did not mention: "And when he recites, then listen attentively."

As for their argument from His saying, ﴿And when the Qur'an is recited, listen to it and be silent﴾ [Surat al-A'raf: 204], it will come in its proper place, God willing.

End of the surah, and success is from God.
